hinweis: The order's greatest philosopher on the architecture the Exercises presuppose: one soul in which sense, imagination and intellect are rooted (II.3), the seven names of the inner sense — sensus communis, phantasia, imaginatio, aestimativa, cogitativa, memoria, reminiscentia — reduced to a single power (III.30), and the intellect that in this life cannot work without a phantasm (IV.7): why composing a place with the imagination is not a preliminary to the understanding's prayer but its condition. Part of the concordance and the citation-bound dialogue; not part of the linguistic statistics, which describe the core corpus only.

sections.titel: Lib. II, cap. III — Utrum potentiae animae fluant ab anima et in ea subjectentur

units.en: St. Thomas treats this question in the first part, question 77, article 4. We, however, shall speak concerning it first of the order and causality of the soul with respect to its powers; secondly of the order and causality which the powers observe among themselves. What of final and formal causality. — As to the first, it is certain that the soul, or the animate thing, is the final cause of the powers; for the powers are ordered to the perfect state of the living thing, as are its operations too: whence although the powers are essentially ordered to operations, nevertheless, because they are at the same time instruments of some operating subject, they do not regard bare operations, but through the medium of the subject whose instruments and virtues they are — and to this they are principally ordered. Concerning formal causality, secondly, it is certain that it does not belong to the soul with respect to the powers; rather the powers themselves are in a certain manner forms of the soul, or of the animate thing, in which they are subjected.
units.orig: Tractat quaestionem hanc D. Thomas, 1. p., quaest. 77, art. 4. Nos vero circa illam primo dicemus de ordine et causalitate animae respectu potentiarum. Secundo de ordine et causalitate, quam ipsae inter se observant. Quid de causalitate finali et formali. — Quantum ad primum certum est, animam, seu animatum esse causam finalem potentiarum; ordinantur enim potentiae ad perfectum statum viventis, sicut et operationes ipsae: unde licet potentiae essentialiter ordinentur ad operationes, tamen quia simul sunt instrumenta alicujus operantis, non nudas operationes respiciunt, sed medio subjecto, cujus sunt instrumenta et virtutes, et ad hoc principaliter ordinantur. De causalitate formali secundo est certum non competere animae respectu potentiarum, quin potius quodammodo ipsae potentiae sunt formae animae, vel animati, in quo subjectantur.
units.label: Quotupliciter anima causet suas potentias

units.en: What, secondly, of the material cause. — It is certain, thirdly, as to the material cause, that the spiritual powers — the intellect, namely, and the will, and any motive power there may be of the soul alone — are subjected immediately in the soul, and so are caused by it materially: but with the other powers it is not so, either because the soul is not subsistent, as in brutes, or because it is not a subject proportioned to such powers, since the soul is spiritual and those powers material. Wherefore Gregory was deceived, on book 2, distinction 17, question 3, in saying that all the sensitive powers — if indeed he distinguished them from the soul — are subjected immediately in the soul itself, and thus that sensation, like intellection, is accomplished in the soul itself; for from this it follows that sensation and sense are spiritual things, nay even the sensible species too, which is impossible, since they are impressed by material things. Again it follows either that brutes do not sense, or that they have spiritual souls, for they will have operations of their own, not exercised in the body. Moreover the diversity of organs for the diverse sensitive powers shows that these are not in the soul but in the organs. Whence nature furnished the intellect with no organ; and Aristotle, in book 2 of De anima, text 122, says the sensorium is the first subject in which sense itself resides, and in book 1, chapter 1, that all the operations and the sensitive powers are common, and of the whole compound. Finally St. Thomas also reports, above at article 8, from the book On the Dogmas of the Church, that man consists of two substances, the soul with its reason and the flesh with its senses. And that word of Paul favors this: The flesh lusts against the spirit, Galatians 5. Gregory presses: otherwise the senses would not remain in the separated soul; and God could preserve them in a dead body, and so it could sense. But the last consequence is denied, because to sense is a vital operation intrinsically dependent on the first principle of life, whence it is impossible for it to exist without it.
units.orig: Quid de materiali secundo. — Est tertio certum quoad causam materialem potentias spirituales, intellectum scilicet et voluntatem, et si qua est potentia motiva solius animae, subjectari immediate in anima, atque adeo ab ea causari materialiter: circa alias vero potentias non sic, vel quia anima non est subsistens, ut in brutis, vel quia non est subjectum proportionatum talibus potentiis, quia anima spiritualis est et ipsae potentiae materiales. Quapropter deceptus est Gregorius, in 2, dist. 17, q. 3, dicens omnes potentias sensitivas, si forte illas ab anima distinxit, subjectari immediate in ipsa anima, atque adeo in anima ipsa perfici sensationem, sicut et intellectionem; ex hoc enim sequitur sensationem et sensum esse spiritualia, imo et species etiam sensibiles, quod est impossibile, cum imprimantur a rebus materialibus. Rursus sequitur vel bruta non sentire, vel animas habere spirituales, nam habebunt operationes proprias, non exercitas in corpore. Praeterea diversitas organorum ad diversas potentias sensitivas ostendit eas non esse in anima, sed in organis. Unde intellectui nullum organum praebuit natura, et Aristoteles 2, de Anima, text. 122, ait sensorium esse primum subjectum, in quo est ipse sensus, et libr. 1, cap. 1, operationes omnes, et potentias sensitivas esse communes, et totius conjuncti. Denique refert etiam divus Thomas, supra articul. 8, ex libr. de Ecclesiasticis dogmatibus, hominem duabus constare substantiis, anima cum ratione sua, et carne cum sensibus suis. Et favet illud Pauli: Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, Gal. 5. Instat Gregorius quia alias sensus non manerent in anima separata, possetque Deus conservare illos in corpore mortuo, itaque posset sentire. Negatur tamen ultima consequentia, quia sentire operatio vitalis est intrinsece dependens a primo principio vitae, unde impossibile est esse sine illo.

units.en: St. Thomas's opinion on the material cause of the material powers reduced to a sound sense. — But you will ask what is the subject of these faculties. St. Thomas says it is the whole composite, and he speaks consistently, since he holds that no accidents are in prime matter. Nevertheless it must be said that these powers are subjected in the composite just insofar as they presuppose it constituted: for they cannot exist unless matter is first informed by the soul, from which they then arise: but to be in the composite in such wise as to inhere in both its parts is impossible, for since they are corporeal accidents they inhere by means of quantity, and so in the subject of quantity, which is matter.
units.orig: Sententia D. Thomae de causa materiali potentiarum materialium reducitur ad bonum sensum. — Sed quaeres, quodnam sit subjectum harum facultatum: S. Thomas ait esse totum compositum, et consequenter loquitur, quia sentit nulla accidentia esse in materia prima. Attamen dicendum has potentias eatenus subjectari in composito, quatenus supponunt ipsum constitutum: non enim possunt esse nisi prius materia informetur anima, ex qua deinde oriantur: at esse in composito, ita ut utrique parti illius inhaereant, est impossibile, nam cum sint accidentia corporalia, inhaerent media quantitate, atque adeo in subjecto quantitatis, quod est materia.

units.en: Concerning the efficient cause the negative side is argued. — About effective causality there are two doubts. First, whether the soul has efficiency with regard to its own powers. Second, if it has it, of what kind it is. On the first, the negative side seems true. First, because the agent, by the same action by which it produces the living thing, produces it with its due powers; for he who gives the form confers what follows upon it: therefore it is superfluous to feign an efficiency between the powers and the soul. This is confirmed: for otherwise two or more actions would have to be feigned in the production of each thing — one, namely, productive of the substantial form, and then others by which the substantial form itself produces the powers: but this seems superfluous, and against that principle that a created substance is not the immediate principle of an action, above all an accidental one. It is confirmed secondly: if the soul had efficiency over its powers, it could by its own power recover them if they were taken away. The consequent is false and against experience: for if sight is once taken away, it does not flow again from the soul. It is confirmed thirdly: the same reasoning holds of the properties of other things as of the powers of the soul; but in other things the properties do not flow effectively from the essence: therefore, etc. The minor is proved: quantity is a property of prime matter, and yet does not flow from it effectively, since matter has no efficiency. Heat too is a property of fire, and yet is not made effectively by its form, since the heat disposing the matter is prior to the form introduced.
units.orig: Circa causam efficientem negativa pars probatur. — De causalitate effectiva duo sunt dubia. Primum, utrum anima habeat efficientiam circa proprias potentias. Secundum, si illam habeat, qualisnam sit. Circa primum videtur pars negativa vera. Primo, quia agens eadem actione, qua producit vivens, ipsum producit cum debitis potentiis, nam qui dat formam, consequentia ad illam confert: ergo superfluum est fingere efficientiam inter potentias et animam. Confirmatur, nam alias duae essent, vel plures fingendae actiones in cujusque rei productione, una scilicet productiva formae substantialis, et deinde aliae, quibus ipsa forma substantialis producit potentias: hoc autem superfluum videtur, et contra illud principium quod substantia creata non sit immediatum principium actionis maxime accidentalis. Confirmatur secundo, quia si anima haberet efficientiam circa suas potentias, posset virtute sua illas recuperare, si auferrentur. Consequens est falsum, et contra experientiam. Nam si semel auferatur visus, non iterum fluit ab anima. Confirmatur tertio. Nam eadem ratio est de proprietatibus aliarum rerum, ac de potentiis animae: sed in rebus aliis proprietates non fluunt effective ab essentia: ergo, etc. Probatur minor: quantitas enim est proprietas materiae primae, et tamen non fluit ab illa effective, cum materia nullam habeat efficientiam. Calor etiam proprietas ignis est, nec tamen fit effective ab illius forma, quia prior est calor disponens materiam, quam forma introducta.

units.en: The affirmative side, following St. Thomas, the more probable. — Nevertheless St. Thomas above, whom the others commonly follow, attributes to the soul efficiency with regard to its powers, which he proves from the difference between proper and common accidents; both indeed require an effective cause, but they differ: the common accidents, being extrinsic, come from an extrinsic cause; but the proper ones, being intrinsic, must come from the intrinsic essence and cause as from an active principle; for the substantial form, which gives the composite its first being simply, must be the efficient cause of the rest that belongs to it per se — for among things ordered per se, what is prior must be the cause of what is posterior; and form and powers are per se ordered to the perfect being of the composite. And this opinion is confirmed, because the essence of a thing has a fuller causality over its own proper passions than over the common accidents; but in regard to the common accidents it is a material and a final cause (for these too are for the perfection of the substance): therefore it has another kind of causality over its proper passions, which can only be effective: therefore, etc. Again, the intellect emanates from the soul more necessarily than heat from heat; but one heat is made effectively by another: therefore a fortiori the intellect will be from the soul efficiently. Again, a necessary connection between two things cannot be without some causality inducing that connection; but material causality taken by itself does not induce it, as appears in an accident and its common subject. And the same account holds of the final cause: therefore this twofold causality does not suffice for so necessary a union as there is between the powers and the essence: therefore another causality must be admitted, and not the formal: therefore the effective. You will say: a relation and its term have a mutual connection, and no causality intervenes there. But it must be answered that between the term taken materially and the relation there is not that mutual connection, since that which terminates can remain without the relation, though not precisely as actually terminating, because as such it depends on it intrinsically in the genus of formal cause. The relation itself too depends in a certain way on the term, as on an extrinsic form, because its essence consists in an order to it: universally, then, a necessary connection depends on some kind of causality. It is confirmed finally from experience: when coldness is taken from water, at once another emanates from the form, and the like holds of other things: therefore the substantial form has efficiency over its properties: therefore with better reason will the soul have it over its powers.
units.orig: Pars affirmativa juxta D. Thomam probabilior. — Nihilominus divus Thomas supra, quem communiter alii sequuntur, tribuunt animae efficientiam circa potentias suas, quod probat ex differentia inter accidentia propria et communia; utraque enim requirunt causam effectivam, sed differunt: quoad accidentia communia, quia extrinseca sunt, proveniunt ab extrinseca causa: at vero propria, quia intrinseca, ab intrinseca essentia et causa provenire debent, tanquam a principio activo; forma enim substantialis, quae dat primum esse simpliciter composito, debet esse causa efficiens reliquorum, quae per se illi conveniunt, nam in per se ordinatis, quod prius est, debet esse causa posterioris; forma autem et potentiae per se ordinantur ad perfectum esse compositi. Et confirmatur haec sententia, quia pleniorem causalitatem habet essentia rei circa proprias passiones suas, quam circa accidentia communia; sed in ordine ad accidentia communia est causa materialis et finalis (sunt enim et haec propter perfectionem substantiae): ergo genus aliud causalitatis habet circa proprias passiones, non nisi effectivae: ergo, etc. Item magis necessario dimanat intellectus ab anima, quam calor a calore: sed unus calor effective fit ab alio: ergo a fortiori intellectus ab anima erit efficienter. Item necessaria connexio inter duo non potest esse absque aliqua causalitate inducente ipsam connexionem; causalitas autem materialis per se sumpta non eam inducit, ut patet in accidenti et subjecto communi. Eademque ratio est de causa finali: ergo duplex ejusmodi causalitas non sufficit ad tam necessariam unionem, quanta est inter potentias et essentiam: ergo admittenda est alia causalitas, et non formalis: ergo effectiva. Dices, relationem et terminum habere mutuam connexionem, nec intervenire ibi causalitatem. Sed occurrendum inter terminum materialiter sumptum et relationem non esse illam mutuam connexionem, cum possit manere id quod terminat sine relatione, quamvis non prout actu terminat, quia ut sic ab ea intrinsece pendet in genere causae formalis. Relatio quoque ipsa pendet a termino quodammodo, ut a forma extrinseca, quia ejus essentia consistit in ordine ad illum: in universum igitur necessaria connexio pendet ab aliquo genere causalitatis. Confirmatur tandem ab experientia. Nam sublata frigiditate ab aqua statim alia dimanat a forma, ac simile est de aliis: ergo forma substantialis habet efficientiam circa proprietates suas: ergo potiori ratione habebit illam anima circa potentias.

units.en: The mode in which the soul is said to effect its powers is inquired into. — The first way of speaking. — But before we resolve this first part of the doubt, let us see what can be said about the second. For if the soul has efficiency, what mode of it, pray, does it have? Some attribute so great an efficiency to it as to assert that the soul produces the powers by a new action, distinct from that by which it was itself produced: and so they pronounce that when the rational soul is created, the creation terminates at the substance of the soul only, and that then the intellect and the will proceed from the soul by another new action — in the way in which the production of the sun by God terminated at the sun only, and in the same instant the sun by another action illuminated the air. And this opinion is argued thus. The rational form has efficiency over its powers really distinct from itself, as was shown in the preceding number: therefore as the soul is an effect of God, so the powers are new effects made by the soul itself; but where there is a new effect there is a new action (for an action is the very thing that comes to be, insofar as it goes forth from the principle of acting): therefore, etc. Secondly, the powers are truly produced by the soul: therefore they are produced by a new action, for to produce without a production is not intelligible. Thirdly, the soul does not concur effectively in its own production, but does concur effectively in the production of the powers, as has been proved: therefore the production of the soul and that of the powers are distinct: therefore the action too is distinct. Fourthly, efficiency intrinsically includes action — it is indeed the mode of causing through action proper to the efficient cause, and therein it is distinguished from the causality of the other causes: therefore if the powers truly emanate effectively from the soul, plainly they emanate from it by means of an action. Fifthly, this emanation would perhaps not be a new action, because once the soul is posited the powers result by natural sequel; but this is no obstacle, since when a certain mixture of the primary qualities is posited the secondary ones too arise through a new action, and when the sun is posited, as we were saying, light follows in the air through an action likewise distinct: therefore natural sequel does not exclude a proper action.
units.orig: Disquiritur modus quo anima suas potentias dicitur efficere. — Primus dicendi modus. — Sed antequam hanc primam partem dubii resolvamus, videamus quid dici possit circa secundam. Nam si anima habet efficientiam, quem ejus modum, quaeso, habet? Quidam tantam efficientiam ei tribuunt, ut asserant animam nova actione producere potentias, atque distincta ab illa, per quam ipsa fuit producta: itaque pronuntiant, cum anima rationalis creatur, creationem terminari ad substantiam animae tantum, et deinde ab anima prodire intellectum et voluntatem nova alia actione: eo modo, quo productio Solis a Deo terminata est ad solem tantum, et in eodem instanti sol alia actione illuminavit aerem. Probaturque haec sententia. Nam forma rationalis habet efficientiam circa suas potentias realiter a se distinctas, ut numero praecedenti ostensum est: ergo sicut anima est effectus Dei, ita potentiae sunt novi effectus ab ipsa anima facti; sed ubi est novus effectus, est nova actio (actio enim res ipsa est, quae fit prout egreditur a principio agendi): ergo, etc. Secundo potentiae vere producuntur ab anima: ergo nova actione producuntur: nam producere sine productione intelligibile non est. Tertio anima non concurrit effective ad sui productionem: concurrit autem effective ad productionem potentiarum, ut est probatum: ergo distincta productio est animae et potentiarum: ergo et actio distincta. Quarto efficientia intrinsece includit actionem, est siquidem modus causandi per actionem proprius causae efficientis, in eoque distinguitur a causalitate caeterarum causarum: ergo si potentiae vere effective dimanant ab anima, plane ab illa media actione dimanant. Quinto haec dimanatio nova actio forte non esset, quia posita semel anima, naturali sequela potentiae resultant; sed hoc non obstat, cum posita etiam certa mixtione primarum qualitatum oriantur secundae per novam actionem, et posito sole, ut dicebamus, sequatur lumen in aere per distinctam etiam actionem: ergo naturalis sequela propriam actionem non excludit.

units.en: The foregoing mode does not please the Thomists. — And it is confirmed. — Nevertheless most of the Thomists reject this way of speaking, because it seems to conflict with two principles which they observe with great religion. The first, that a created substance cannot be the immediate principle of any action, above all an accidental one; and so it is impossible that the soul should cause the powers through an action proceeding immediately from itself. The second principle is that nothing can act upon itself per se and primarily: since therefore the soul receives the powers in itself, such as the intellect and the will, it does not properly act them in itself, and hence not by means of an action either. On account of these things Cajetan above, and more at large on the first part, question 54, article 3 — whom others follow — says that the powers emanate from their own form without any action, by a certain resultancy; and St. Thomas favors him above, in the replies to the second and third objections, where he says the soul is the active principle of the powers not properly but in a certain manner, because it does not effect them by a proper transmutation but by a certain resultancy. And it is confirmed: otherwise there would be per se motion or mutation toward the soul's powers, for there is per se motion and mutation toward that thing to which a proper productive action per se tends: but the consequent is against Aristotle: wherefore, etc.
units.orig: Non placet Thomistis praedictus modus. — Et confirmatur. — Nihilominus plerique Thomistarum rejiciunt hunc dicendi modum, quod pugnare videatur duobus principiis, quae ipsi magna religione observant. Primum, quod substantia creata nequeat esse immediatum principium alicujus actionis, maxime accidentalis, atque adeo impossibile sit animam per actionem a se immediate prodeuntem causare potentias. Secundum principium est, nihil posse agere in seipsum per se primo: cum ergo anima recipiat in se potentias, ut intellectum et voluntatem, eas proprie in se non agit, ac proinde nec media actione. Propter haec Cajetanus supra, et latius 1 p., q. 54, art. 3, quem alii sequuntur, ait potentias dimanare a propria forma sine ulla actione per quamdam resultantiam, cui favet D. Thomas supra, ad 2 et 3, ubi ait animam esse principium activum potentiarum non proprie, sed quodammodo, quia non efficit propria transmutatione, sed per resultantiam quamdam. Et confirmatur, quia alias ad potentias animae daretur per se motus, seu mutatio, nam ad rem illam est per se motus et mutatio, ad quam propria actio productiva per se tendit: consequens autem est contra Aristotelem: quare, etc.

units.en: Notes toward the decision. — For the resolution it must be noted that it belongs to the notion of a passion to have an inseparable union with the substance of the thing, so far as lies in itself; which I add for this reason, that some separability which comes about from without does not take away the character of a property; the highest heat, for instance, is a property of fire though separable from it, for in that separation the fire is at least incipiently corrupted and dragged outside the state due to its nature. Secondly it must be noted that properties always belong to a thing by reason of its form, as St. Thomas said (I except quantity, which is the peculiar property of matter): among the properties required for the sake of the form, then, some are required not only as following upon the form but also as prior, for inducing it: of this sort are the dispositions, which at least in nature precede the form in the matter. Others are properties which presuppose the existence of the thing and are attributed to it as virtues for operating; such are the powers of the soul, above all the sensitive and intellective, and many virtues too of herbs and minerals. And between these and those properties there is this difference, that the former are not made effectively by the form in the first instant of generation, but immediately by the agent disposing the matter that the form may be induced — which the third confirmation made above in the fourth number proves, and it concludes plainly on the supposition of the other opinion, that accidents are in prime matter; for thence it follows that no ultimate disposition is made by the form but by the agent, although the form itself would not of itself lack the virtue to cause that disposition, since if it is perchance taken away the form at once effects another: in the first instant therefore it does not effect it, because it finds it made, and thereafter only conserves it.
units.orig: Notationes pro decisione. — Pro resolutione est notandum de ratione passionis esse inseparabilem unionem cum substantia rei, quantum de se est; quod ideo addo, quoniam aliqualis separabilitas, quae ab extrinseco fit, non tollit rationem proprietatis; est enim summus calor, verbi gratia, proprietas ignis, licet sit separabilis ab illo, nam in ea separatione ignis saltem inchoate corrumpitur, atque extra statum naturae suae debitum trahitur. Secundo est notandum proprietates semper convenire rei ratione formae, ut D. Thomas dixit (quantitatem excipio, quae est individua proprietas materiae): inter proprietates ergo gratia formae requisitas quaedam requiruntur non solum ut consequentes formam, sed etiam ut praeviae ad illam inducendam: hujusmodi vero sunt dispositiones, quae formam saltem natura praecedunt in materia. Aliae sunt proprietates, quae supponunt existentiam rei, et illi tribuuntur, tanquam virtutes ad operandum, quales sunt potentiae animae, maxime sensitivae et intellectivae, et multae etiam virtutes herbarum et mineralium. Atque inter has et illas proprietates illud interest, quod priores illae non fiant effective a forma in primo instanti generationis, sed immediate ab agente disponente materiam, ut inducatur forma, quod probat tertia confirmatio supra facta numero quarto, quae concludit plane supposita alia sententia, quod accidentia sint in materia prima; inde namque sequitur nullam ultimam dispositionem fieri a forma, sed ab agente, quanquam formae ipsi de se non deesset virtus ad illam dispositionem causandam, siquidem ea forte ablata statim efficit aliam: in primo ergo instanti non efficit, quia factam invenit, tantumque deinceps conservat.

units.en: First pronouncement on the doubt posed in number 4. — Of the other properties, which follow the form and are simply posterior to it in every genus of cause — and about these the principal question proceeds — the opinion of St. Thomas seems very probable. First, because that intimate union which is found between the form and the virtues seems necessarily to induce between them some effective causality; for the other causalities by no means suffice. Secondly, those properties which are once taken away and flow forth again show that between form and property there is this kind of causality. Thirdly, since the soul is simply prior to its properties, it is consonant with reason that it should have that order of causality with respect to them: therefore.
units.orig: Primum pronuntiatum circa dubium positum n. 4. — De aliis vero proprietatibus, quae consequuntur formam, ac simpliciter ea posteriores sunt in omni genere causae, de quibus praecipua quaestio procedit, videtur valde probabilis opinio D. Thomae. Primo, quia illa intima unio, quae inter formam et virtutes reperitur, videtur necessario inducere inter illas aliquam causalitatem effectivam; aliae namque causalitates minime sufficiunt. Secundo proprietates illae, quae semel auferuntur, et iterum manant, ostendunt esse inter formam et proprietatem hoc genus causalitatis. Tertio, cum anima sit simpliciter prior suis proprietatibus, rationi consonum est, ut illum ordinem causalitatis habeat respectu illarum: ergo.

units.en: Second pronouncement. — Third. — Whence I say secondly that consequently it seems to be granted that the action productive of a thing terminates immediately at its substance, taken precisely apart from the properties. Thirdly I say that that action productive of the substance is distinct from the one by which the power itself emanates from the soul: both of these are plain from the arguments made against the opinion of the Thomists in the sixth number, and this is explained and urged again. For imagine God creating the substance of the soul while impeding the emanation of the power from it — that this can be done was shown above: the substance of the soul would then remain without intellect and will; but let God afterwards remove the impediment and leave the soul to its own nature — certainly the intellect and the will would emanate from it, just as in the first instant of generation or creation. Now one argues thus: in that case the creative action would have its complete term, which would be nothing other than the substance of the soul alone; but the emanation of intellect and will following afterwards would be a distinct action, as separated even in time from the creation, and producing something new: therefore now too the same actions exist in the instant of creation, for what in the case supposed are separated in time, the mind must separate by its act in one instant; for that they happen together does not take away the distinction. It is confirmed first: either the powers too are produced by force of the action productive of the soul, or not. If the first: then since that whole action is from the agent, the soul effects nothing at all in the production of its powers, which is absurd. If the second: then there must be another action through which the power is produced. It is confirmed secondly: an action per se one must terminate at one per se term; but the soul with its powers is one by aggregation: therefore that whole is not produced by one action. This is more easily understood in the production of material forms, for such an action is eductive of the substantial form out of the potency of matter; and eduction, considered in its own nature, terminates formally only at the substantial form: therefore the following of the properties from the form cannot be understood without a new action — which is clearer still in the adduced case of the emanation of the powers separated from the production of the form, and is plain too in water bringing itself back to its former cold. For that motion is truly made by the substantial form of the water, and the action of chilling is no less true than if it came from without — for what difference does it make? Whence it must be considered that when a form's properties are dispositions prior to it, they too are made by an action distinct from that by which the form, posterior in nature, is induced — namely by the dispositive alteration; yet with this difference, that such dispositions proceed not from the form as from an active principle but immediately from the agent, while the properties that follow the form draw their origin from it.
units.orig: Secundum pronuntiatum. — Tertium. — Unde dico secundo, consequenter videri concedendum actionem productivam rei immediate terminari ad substantiam ipsius, ut praecisam a proprietatibus. Tertio dico actionem illam productivam substantiae distinctam esse ab illa, qua potentia ipsa dimanat ab anima: utrumque istorum patet factis argumentis contra opinionem Thomistarum in numero sexto, quod iterum explicatur et suadetur. Nam finge Deum creare substantiam animae impediendo emanationem potentiae ab illa, hoc enim posse fieri supra est ostensum: maneret ergo tunc substantia animae absque intellectu et voluntate; auferat vero postea Deus impedimentum, relinquatque animam suae naturae, certe dimanarent ab illa intellectus atque voluntas, sicut in primo instanti generationis aut creationis. Jam sic arguitur: in eo casu actio creativa haberet suum terminum integrum, qui alius non esset, quam sola animae substantia; intellectus vero ac voluntatis dimanatio postea subsequens esset distincta actio, utpote separata etiam tempore a creatione, et aliquid novum producens: ergo et nunc eaedem actiones sunt in instanti creationis, nam quae in casu posito separantur tempore, debet mens in uno instanti per actum separare; quod enim simul fiant, distinctionem non aufert. Confirmatur primo. Nam vel ex vi actionis productivae animae producuntur etiam potentiae, vel non. Si primum: ergo cum tota illa actio sit ab agente, anima nihil omnino efficit in productione suarum potentiarum, quod est absurdum. Si secundum: ergo debet alia esse actio, per quam potentia producatur. Confirmatur secundo. Nam actio per se una debet terminari ad unum per se terminum: at vero anima cum potentiis est unum per aggregationem: ergo totum illud per unam actionem non producitur. Id quod facilius intelligitur in productione formarum materialium, nam talis actio est eductiva formae substantialis de potentia materiae: eductio vero ex propriis considerata formaliter tantum terminatur ad substantialem formam: ergo consecutio proprietatum a forma non potest intelligi sine nova actione, quod clarius adhuc patet in allato casu separatae dimanationis potentiarum a productione formae, ac patet etiam in aqua reducente se ad pristinum frigus. Nam vere motus ille fit a forma substantiali aquae, nec minus vera actio frigefaciendi est, quam si proveniret ab extrinseco, quid enim refert? Unde est considerandum, quando formae proprietates sunt dispositiones illa priores, fieri etiam distincta actione ab ea, qua posterius natura inducitur forma, alteratione videlicet dispositiva; eo tamen discrimine, quod tales dispositiones non a forma tanquam a principio activo, sed immediate ab agente procedunt: at proprietates consequentes formam suam originem ab illa ducunt.

units.en: Fourth pronouncement. — Yet I say fourthly: absolutely speaking it must be said that the principal agent produces the form with all the virtues that follow from it. This certainly is the common way of speaking and of thinking of all; thus God, in creating the soul, is said to concreate the powers. The reason is that it belongs to the agent to produce the substance of a thing furnished through and through for its end, and therefore in giving the form it gives everything that perfects it, not only as to being but also that it may be an exact principle of operating, and so a principle of the powers required for the end of operating. Again, the generator intends to assimilate the begotten to itself as much as it can: that action, then, by which it induces the form, though immediately it is inductive of the form only, is mediately and radically comproductive of everything that naturally and necessarily follows from it, as pertaining to the perfection of the begotten. In this sense it is customarily said, and truly, that there is a single action productive of the thing and comproductive of the properties, because they are not considered with precision, but the radical and primary action is considered. And through these things the solution of the arguments is plain.
units.orig: Quartum pronuntiatum. — Dico tamen quarto: absolute dicendum est, agens principale producere formam cum omnibus virtutibus, quae ex illa sequuntur. Hic certe est communis modus loquendi et sentiendi omnium; sic Deus creando animam dicitur potentias concreare. Ratio vero est, quia agentis est producere substantiam rei usquequaque instructam ad suum finem, et ideo dando formam dat omnia, quae ipsam perficiunt, non tantum quoad esse, sed etiam ut sit exactum principium operandi, atque adeo ut sit principium potentiarum ad finem operandi requisitarum. Item generans intendit assimilare sibi genitum quantum potest: illa ergo actio, qua formam inducit, licet immediate tantum sit inductiva formae, mediate et radicaliter est comproductiva omnium, quae naturaliter et necessario ex illa sequuntur, tanquam ad perfectionem geniti attinentia. Quo sensu dici solet, ac vere, unicam esse actionem productivam rei, et comproductivam proprietatum, quia non considerantur cum praecisione, sed consideratur actio radicalis et primaria. Et per haec patet solutio argumentorum.

units.en: To the arguments in number 4. — To the first we say that the agent by one action produces everything mediately or immediately, and that the axiom is to be expounded thus: he who gives the form gives — namely in the root — what follows upon the form. To the first confirmation it is answered that, considering the matter precisely, there are as many actions as entities; yet it is called a single action because from it the rest emanate. The second confirmation does not press us in particular: for of itself it raises its own difficulty, why the powers of the soul, once separated, do not flow again, as we experience happens in water and in the other natural virtues of inanimate things. And it can be answered first that nature foresaw what is in things per se, not what is per accidens: and it is per se that a property which has a contrary is somewhat diminished by it, and therefore nature gave the substantial form strength to recover such a loss; but the powers of the soul have of themselves no contrary, and therefore can of themselves last as long as the soul itself can: while it is per accidens that they are sometimes weakened from elsewhere, and therefore nature did not provide for that. Yet this answer does not seem to satisfy, for if the soul is a virtue for effecting its powers, that virtue is not diminished by its having once effected them. It must be said, then, that the powers of the soul are in fact not injured or taken away except when the organs in which they reside are injured or taken away — which organs are substances, and their subjects: since therefore the soul cannot recover a lost organ, as neither can it recover a cut-off hand, neither therefore the power subjected in the organ. To the third answer has already been given: as to the point about prime matter, we spoke in the book On Generation, first disputation, question 4, about the second confirmation of the eighth argument of the second opinion; and the second solution there given is more conformable to the doctrine here delivered, though the first too can be sustained, because there is a special reason in matter on account of its potentiality.
units.orig: Ad argumenta in n. 4. — Ad primum enim dicimus agens una actione producere omnia mediate, vel immediate, sicque exponi illud axioma: Qui dat formam, dare, scilicet in radice, consequentia ad formam. Ad primam confirmationem respondetur, rem praecise considerando tot esse actiones, quot entitates; dici tamen unicam actionem, quod ex illa reliquae dimanent. Secunda confirmatio nos non urget speciatim: per se enim propriam difficultatem postulat, cur potentiae animae semel separatae non iterum fluant, sicut experimur fieri in aqua, et in aliis naturalibus virtutibus inanimatorum. Et responderi potest primo, naturam praevidisse id, quod per se est in rebus, non quod per accidens: per se autem esse, quod proprietas habens contrarium ab illo minuatur aliquantulum, ideoque naturam dedisse formae substantiali vires ad recuperandum tale detrimentum; potentias vero animae de se non habere contrarium, et ideo de se tamdiu posse durare, quamdiu et ipsa anima possit: per accidens vero esse, quod aliquando debilitentur aliunde, ideoque naturam id non providisse. Haec tamen responsio non videtur facere satis, nam si anima est virtus ad efficiendas suas potentias, quod semel illas efficiat, ea virtus non minuitur. Dicendum ergo potentias animae de facto non laedi, vel auferri, nisi laesis, aut ablatis organis, in quibus resident, quae organa substantiae sunt, ac subjecta illarum: quia ergo anima ablatum organum non potest recuperare, sicut nec recuperare abscissam manum, ideo neque potentiam in organo subjectatam. Ad tertium jam responsum est: ad illud vero de materia prima diximus in libro de Generatione, disputatione prima, quaest. 4, circa secundam confirmationem octavi argumenti secundae opinionis, et secunda solutio ibi data est conformior doctrinae hic traditae, quamvis etiam prima sustineri possit, quia est specialis ratio in materia propter ipsius potentialitatem.

units.en: To the motives of the Thomists in number 7. — To the confirmation at the end of the same number 7. — To the motive of the Thomists it is answered that those two principles are not so irrefragable; yet they can here be expounded according to the mind of St. Thomas, namely that the substantial form is not the immediate principle of perfecting its own suppositum, at least in first act — and this perhaps St. Thomas intended; or say that the form is not active except by the action naturally resulting from it, which is called emanation: and this, if it is effective, can hardly be understood without an action. Similarly it is said to the other principle that the same thing does not act upon itself except by this genus of action which is emanation, or at any rate acts only as the virtue of the generator: but of this second principle we have said more elsewhere. To the confirmation it is answered first that there is per se motion toward something when there is given in nature an action tending per se and primarily toward it, but not if the action is as an emanation from another action; for when many things follow from the force of one action, although there is an order among them, and considering one with respect to another there is a new action between them, still a new action is not said to be among them except toward that to which it tends first and radically: so then stands the matter in the case proposed. Secondly it is said that it is one thing for an action to tend per se to some term, another for there to be per se primary motion toward it: it can therefore be conceded that toward these powers there is in some way a per se action, but not properly a mutation, because their subject is not changed, since they begin to be together with it; and a thing is properly said to come to be through mutation when it comes to be with a change of the subject. And so much for the first part of the question.
units.orig: Ad motiva Thomistarum in n. 7. — Ad confirmationem in fine ejusdem num. 7. — Ad motivum Thomistarum respondetur, illa duo principia non esse adeo irrefragabilia; attamen exponi hic posse ad mentem sancti Thomae, quod forma substantialis non sit immediatum principium perficiendi suum suppositum saltem in actu primo, et hoc forte intendit divus Thomas; vel dicito formam non esse activam nisi actione naturaliter resultante ex illa, quae dicitur dimanatio: haec autem, si effectiva est, sine actione difficile intelligi potest. Similiter dicitur ad alterum principium, quod idem in se non agat praeterquam hoc actionis genere, quae est dimanatio, vel certe non agit nisi ut virtus generantis: sed de hoc secundo principio plura diximus alio loco. Ad confirmationem respondetur primo tunc esse per se motum ad aliquid, quando datur actio in natura per se primo tendens ad illud, non vero si actio sit tanquam dimanatio ab alia actione; quando enim multa sequuntur ex vi unius actionis, quamvis inter alia sit ordo, et considerando unum respectu alterius, sit nova actio inter ea, non dicitur tamen inter ea nova actio, nisi ad id ad quod primo et radicaliter ipsa tendit: sic ergo res habet in proposito. Secundo dicitur aliud esse actionem tendere per se ad terminum aliquem, aliud vero, esse ad illum per se primo motum: potest ergo concedi ad has potentias esse aliquo modo actionem per se, non vero proprie mutationem, quia subjectum earum non mutatur, cum simul incipiant esse cum illo; proprie vero res dicitur per mutationem fieri, quando fit cum subjecti mutatione. Et haec de prima parte quaestionis.

units.en: A note. — On the second part of this chapter, which we proposed at its very beginning — namely on the order of the powers among themselves — it must first be noted briefly that it is an almost certain matter that some order is kept among the powers of the soul; for, as St. Thomas excellently observes, when many things arise from one they must proceed in order, not confusedly and as it were tumultuously: and such an order can be understood either between the powers themselves, or by respect to some one third thing. Between themselves, as the cognitive and the appetitive powers; for the latter are plainly subordinated to the former: as in operating (for nothing is willed unless foreknown), so also in being. By respect to one third thing, as the sensitive powers, so manifold, exist for our sake, and are directed to this, that we may have perfect knowledge of sensible things. Secondly it must be noted that the aforesaid order can be manifold: namely of duration, as though one power existed later than another, or than the soul itself; or of dignity, because some powers are worthier than others; or of generation, because some powers proceed before others; or of objects, because their objects are prior to others according to their own nature, as the visible before the audible; or of end, insofar as one power is ordered to another as to an end, namely to minister to it, as the exterior senses serve the interior; or finally of effective emanation, so that one power should emanate from another immediately. Thirdly it must be noted that the powers which follow the soul according to one and the same grade are compared either among themselves or to the powers following according to another grade — as the vegetative among themselves, or in order to the sensitive, and both in order to the intellective.
units.orig: Notatio. — Circa secundam partem hujus capitis, quam ipso initio proposuimus, scilicet de ordine potentiarum inter se, notandum primo est breviter, esse rem fere certam inter potentias animae aliquem servari ordinem; nam, ut D. Thomas optime advertit, quando plura oriuntur ab uno, debent ordinatim procedere, non confuse, ac veluti tumultuatim: potest autem talis ordo intelligi, vel inter potentias ipsas, vel per respectum ad unum tertium. Inter se quidem, ut potentiae cognoscitivae et appetitivae; hae namque illis plane subordinantur: sicut in operando (nihil enim volitum, quin praecognitum), ita et in essendo. Per respectum vero ad unum tertium, ut tam multiplices potentiae sensitivae nostri gratia sunt, et ad hoc diriguntur ut cognitionem perfectam sensibilium habeamus. Secundo notandum, praedictum ordinem esse posse multiplicem: scilicet vel durationis, quasi una potentia posterius existat, quam alia, vel quam anima ipsa: vel dignitatis, quia potentiae quaedam sunt digniores aliis: vel generationis, quia potentiae aliae priores aliis procedunt: vel objectorum, quia earum objecta sunt priora aliis secundum naturam suam, ut visibile, quam audibile: vel finis, quatenus una potentia ordinatur ad aliam, ut ad finem, ut scilicet illi ministret, ut exteriores sensus deserviunt interioribus: vel denique emanationis effectivae, ita ut una potentia emanet ab alia immediate. Tertio est notandum comparari potentias, quae consequuntur animam secundum unum et eumdem gradum, vel inter se, vel ad potentias consequentes secundum alium gradum, ut vegetativas inter se, aut in ordine ad sensitivas, et utrasque in ordine ad intellectivas.
units.label: De ordine et causalitate, quam potentiae inter se servant resultando ab anima

units.en: First pronouncement in this second part of the chapter. — Second pronouncement. — Third pronouncement. — Fourth pronouncement. — Fifth pronouncement. — This presupposed, I say first: in the order of duration there is no order among the powers of the same living thing, either among themselves or with the soul from which they flow. It is plain, because all begin in the same instant, for all emanate from one soul, which begins to be in one and the same instant — as is openly to be seen in man. I say secondly: in the order of generation the powers that follow the soul according to an imperfect grade are prior in nature to the others. It is proved: the soul according to its more imperfect grade is prior in nature to itself according to the perfect grade: therefore the powers proportionally too. Again, the acts of those powers are prior — as nutrition to sensation, because sensation depends on nutrition as on a supplier, and the same holds of intellection with respect to sensation: therefore the powers too are prior; and this priority is reduced to the genus of material cause, for the more imperfect grade is compared to the more perfect as potency to act — in which way St. Thomas, above at the seventh article, writes that the more imperfect powers are as it were material causes with respect to the others, because in a certain way they dispose toward them, as the lower grade toward the higher. I say thirdly: the powers of the lower grade are more imperfect than the powers of the higher grade: this is plain by induction and by the natural light itself. I say fourthly: the lower powers are ordered to serving the higher, and the higher to aiding the lower; thus the vegetative powers minister to the sensitive, for they perfect their organs and furnish them strength, that they may better exercise their operations: and the sensitive in turn are ordered to protecting the vegetative powers and to seeking and preparing food for them; and these again, compared to the intellective, are their handmaids, and instruments for acquiring species: while conversely the intellective direct the sensitive and rule over them; and at last all are ordered to the perfect state, conservation and government of the living thing — as in a well-ordered commonwealth the lower serve the higher, and the higher direct and protect the lower, and all exercise their offices, that the commonwealth may be well constituted. You will say: the vegetative powers of themselves are not ordered to the sensitive, as is evident in plants, nor the sensitive to the intellective, as appears in brutes. It is answered that any powers whatever are immediately ordered to their own acts, but can be ultimately ordered to serving the more perfect powers by reason of the more perfect principle from which they emanate — from which they also claim to exercise their own actions in a more perfect way. I say fifthly: among the powers belonging to the same grade of the soul there is also some order from those numbered above. It is proved and explained. For among the powers of the vegetative part, the attractive power serves the retentive, and both the expulsive; these serve the nutritive, which is the disposing virtue, and all at last minister to the assimilative virtue. Again, in animals the cognitive powers beget appetite, and appetite local motion. Among the senses too, the external serve the internal: the external, however, are not ordered among themselves so that one serves another; yet they help one another insofar as one supplies the defect of another, and all together complete one perfect sentient being; for which cause St. Thomas assigned no order among the external senses except on the side of the objects, insofar as one tends to an object prior in itself before another: similarly between intellect and will there is order, because the intellect directs the will and commands it, while the will moves and applies the intellect in free acts. And the universal reason of all these things is that, since all these powers flow forth from the same principle and are ordered to its perfect state, it is fitting that they observe an order among themselves.
units.orig: Primum pronuntiatum in hac secundae capitis parte. — Secundum pronuntiatum. — Tertium pronuntiatum. — Quartum pronuntiatum. — Quintum pronuntiatum. — Hoc supposito dico primo. In ordine durationis nullus est ordo inter potentias ejusdem viventis inter se, vel cum anima, a qua fluunt. Patet, quia omnes incipiunt in eodem instanti, nam omnes dimanant ab una anima, quae in unico eodemque instanti incipit esse: id, quod aperte videre est in homine. Dico secundo. Ordine generationis potentiae, quae consequuntur animam secundum gradum imperfectum, sunt priores secundum naturam, quam aliae. Probatur, quia anima secundum gradum imperfectiorem est natura prior, quam secundum gradum perfectum: ergo et potentiae proportionaliter. Item actus illarum potentiarum sunt priores, ut nutritio sensatione, quia sensatio pendet a nutritione tanquam a subministrante, atque idem est de intellectione respectu sensationis: ergo et potentiae sunt priores; haec vero prioritas ad genus causae materialis reducitur: nam gradus imperfectior comparatur ad perfectiorem, ut potentia ad actum, quomodo divus Thomas supra, articulo septimo, scribit potentias imperfectiores esse velut materiales causas respectu aliarum, quia quodammodo disponunt ad illas, sicut inferior gradus ad superiorem. Dico tertio. Potentiae gradus inferioris sunt imperfectiores potentiis gradus superioris: patet hoc inductione et ipso naturali lumine. Dico quarto. Inferiores potentiae ordinantur ad deserviendum superioribus, superiores vero ad adjuvandum inferiores; sic potentiae vegetativae ministrant sensitivis, nam organa illarum perficiunt, et illis praebent vires, ut melius possint exercere suas operationes: sensitivae vero vicissim ordinantur ad tuendas vegetativas potentias, et ad quaerendum, et praeparandum illis cibum; quae rursum comparatae ad intellectivas ministrae illarum sunt, et instrumenta comparandi species: vicissim vero intellectivae dirigunt sensitivas, eisque dominantur, ac tandem omnes ordinantur ad perfectum viventis statum, conservationem et regimen, sicut in republica bene ordinata inferiores deserviunt superioribus, et superiores dirigunt, et tuentur inferiores, et omnes sua munera exercent, ut respublica bene sit instituta. Dices, potentiae vegetativae de se non ordinantur ad sensitivas, ut in plantis constat, nec sensitivae ad intellectivas, ut patet in brutis. Respondetur, potentias quidem quascumque immediate ordinari ad proprios actus, ultimate vero ordinari posse ad deserviendum perfectioribus potentiis ratione perfectioris principii, a quo dimanant, a quo etiam vendicant, ut actiones proprias perfectiori modo exerceant. Dico quinto. Inter potentias pertinentes ad eumdem gradum animae, etiam est ordo aliquis ex supra numeratis. Probatur et explicatur. Nam inter potentias vegetativae partis, potentia attractiva deservit retentivae, et utraque expulsivae; deserviunt nutritivae, quae est virtus disponens, et omnes tandem ministrant assimilatrici virtuti. Rursum in animantibus potentiae cognoscitivae pariunt appetitum, et appetitus motum localem. Inter sensus quoque, externi deserviunt internis: externi vero inter se non ordinantur, ut unum alteri deserviat; juvant tamen sese quatenus alter defectum alterius supplet, et omnes integrant unum perfectum sentiens; qua de causa D. Thomas inter sensus externos non assignavit ordinem praeterquam ex parte objectorum, quatenus unus tendit in objectum secundum se prius quam alius: similiter inter intellectum et voluntatem ordo est, quia intellectus dirigit voluntatem, eique imperat, voluntas vero movet et applicat intellectum in actibus liberis. Et ratio universalis horum omnium est, quia cum omnes istae potentiae profluant ab eodem principio, et ordinentur ad perfectum illius statum, congruum est, ut inter se ordinem observent.

units.en: What St. Thomas thinks of the mode of emanation of one power from another. — There is, however, a difficulty at this point: whether one power emanates effectively from another in the way in which all emanate from the essence. St. Thomas above asserted universally that the more imperfect powers emanate in that way from the more perfect, and more clearly on the first book, distinction 3, question 4, article 3. This opinion at once appears difficult: for how can it be believed that the vegetative powers of man flow from the rational soul by means of the intellect and the will? Further, one argues ad hominem: the sensitive grade and the powers answering to it are prior to the rational powers, and the vegetative powers prior to both: therefore it is impossible that these powers should arise effectively from those; for things that are active principles are simply prior in the order of existing (for to effect presupposes existing): and things prior in existing are prior in generation, since generation tends toward being: therefore it is impossible that the more imperfect powers — prior in the way of generation and hence in being — should arise actively from the more perfect. And it is confirmed: among the other passions of things no such order of active emanation is found; in air, for instance, heat does not emanate from moisture, nor moisture from heat. Add that this efficiency is asserted by no necessity; for to save the intrinsic connection among the passions it is enough that all be rooted in the same soul, though they have no causality among themselves.
units.orig: Quid de modo emanationis unius potentiae ab alia sentiat D. Thomas. — Est vero difficultas hoc loco, an una potentia dimanet effective ab altera eo modo, quo omnes dimanant ab essentia. D. Thomas supra universaliter asseruit potentias imperfectiores dimanare illo modo a perfectioribus, et clarius in primo, distinctione tertia, quaestione quarta, art. 3. Quae sententia difficilis statim apparet, quomodo enim credi potest potentias vegetativas hominis ab anima rationali mediante intellectu et voluntate manare? Praeterea arguitur ad hominem, nam gradus sensitivus, ac potentiae illi respondentes sunt priores potentiis rationalibus, et vegetativae potentiae priores utrisque: ergo impossibile est, quod hae potentiae effective oriantur ab illis, nam quae sunt principia activa, sunt simpliciter priora in ordine existendi, efficere enim supponit existere: quae vero sunt priora in existendo, sunt priora in generatione, cum generatio tendat ad esse; ergo impossibile est, quod potentiae imperfectiores, ac priores via generationis, atque adeo in essendo, oriantur active a perfectioribus. Et confirmatur. Nam inter alias passiones rerum non invenitur talis ordo dimanationis activae, ut in aere calor non dimanat ab humiditate, vel humiditas a calore. Adde, nulla necessitate astrui hanc efficientiam, nam ad salvandam connexionem intrinsecam inter passiones satis est radicari omnes in eadem anima, quamvis inter se causalitatem non habeant.

units.en: Sixth pronouncement, of a double sense. — Wherefore I say sixthly: one power of the soul does not arise actively from another. This conclusion can be understood either comparing powers of different grades or of the same, and in both ways it holds true: the first part is proved above all by the reasons made in the preceding number. There is besides that the soul, which is the principle of the powers, can be their immediate principle, so far as lies in itself, as appears in plants and brutes: therefore better in man, in whom these grades exist in a more perfect way. And it is confirmed: by the very fact that the soul gives man vegetative being, it can also confer all the powers of that grade, even if such a grade be prescinded from the higher ones. The second part is plain by induction, for hearing does not arise from sight, nor conversely. And the reason can be that a vital power depends in its operation on the principle whence it emanates; but all the powers depend on the soul immediately in operating: therefore all emanate from it; and if one flowed forth from another, it would not operate without the actual concurrence of that other, just as none operates without the actual concurrence of the soul.
units.orig: Sextum pronuntiatum duplicis sensus. — Quapropter dico sexto. Una potentia animae non oritur active ab alia. Haec conclusio potest intelligi aut comparando potentias diversorum graduum, aut ejusdem, et utroque modo habet verum: primamque partem potissime probant rationes factae numero praecedenti. Accedit quod anima, quae principium est potentiarum, potest esse immediatum principium earumdem, quantum est de se, ut patet in plantis ac brutis: ergo melius in homine, in quo hi gradus sunt perfectiori modo. Et confirmatur. Nam eo ipso, quod anima dat homini esse vegetativum, potest et conferre omnes potentias illius gradus, etiamsi praescindatur ejusmodi gradus a superioribus. Secunda pars inductione patet, nam auditus non oritur ex visu, neque e contrario. Et ratio esse potest, quia potentia vitalis pendet in sua operatione a principio, unde dimanat, omnes autem potentiae pendent ab anima immediate in operando: ergo omnes ab illa dimanant, et si una proflueret ab alia, non operaretur sine actuali concursu illius, sicut nulla operatur sine actuali concursu animae.

units.en: First objection against what has just been said. — To the first. — To the second. — To the third. — But against this there are arguments. First, because this is a demonstration a priori: man is rational: therefore he is sensitive: therefore rationality is the cause of sensibility, and only an effective one: therefore. Secondly, the sensitive powers in man are most perfect: therefore this is because they emanate from the intellective. Thirdly, the senses in man are as instruments ministering to the intellect: therefore they emanate from it. To the first it is answered that an argument from the lower to the higher is not properly a demonstration through the cause: for this argumentation — he is a man, therefore he is an animal — is not a priori, since this causal statement is false: because he is a man, therefore he is an animal; for man is not the cause of animal (rather animal is the material cause of man), except perhaps in the genus of final cause, in the way the whole is the cause of its parts, and the more perfect the cause of the less perfect; and in that way we concede the rational to be the cause of the sensitive — not an efficient but a final cause. To the second it is said that the sensitive powers are more perfect in man because they arise from a more perfect soul, and not because from the intellect. To the third it is answered that for that office it is enough if intellect and sense are rooted in the same soul.
units.orig: Prima objectio contra proxime dicta. — Ad primum. — Ad secundum. — Ad tertium. — Sed contra hoc sunt argumenta. Primum, quia haec est demonstratio a priori: homo est rationalis: ergo est sensitivus: ergo rationalitas est causa sensibilitatis, et non nisi effectiva: ergo. Secundo, potentiae sensitivae in homine sunt perfectissimae: ergo ideo est, quia dimanant ab intellectiva. Tertio, sensus in homine sunt tanquam instrumenta ministrantia intellectui: ergo dimanant ab illo. Ad primum respondetur argumentum ab inferiori ad superius non esse proprie demonstrationem per causam: haec enim argumentatio: Est homo, ergo est animal, non est a priori, cum haec causalis sit falsa: quia est homo, ideo est animal; nam homo non est causa animalis (sed potius animal causa est materialis hominis), nisi forte in genere causae finalis, quomodo totum est causa suarum partium, et perfectius causa imperfectioris; eoque modo concedimus rationale esse causam sensitivi, non efficientem, sed finalem. Ad secundum dicitur potentias sensitivas perfectiores esse in homine, quia oriuntur a perfectiori anima, et non quia ab intellectu. Ad tertium respondetur ad id munus satis esse si intellectus et sensus in eadem anima radicentur.

units.en: One note for a fuller understanding of what has been said. — It must nevertheless be observed that between powers belonging to different grades of the soul there is sometimes a greater affinity than between others: intellect and sense, for instance, agree in the genus of cognitive power, in which they do not agree with the vegetative; and therefore they seem to have a greater causality and subordination between themselves, for the sensitive powers are as it were certain participations of the intellective virtue; and of these St. Thomas seems to speak in particular. Yet even in these no proper efficiency is discerned, but a certain as-it-were exemplary causality, since sensitive cognition is a certain imitation of the intellective; in which way too the works of the vegetative part, insofar as they are done as if by art and intellect, can be called its imitations.
units.orig: Notatio una pro uberiori dictorum intelligentia. — Advertendum est tamen inter potentias pertinentes ad diversos gradus animae, aliquando majorem convenientiam dari, quam inter alias: intellectus enim et sensus, verbi gratia, conveniunt in genere cognoscitivae potentiae, in quo non conveniunt cum vegetativis, et ideo illae videntur majorem habere inter se causalitatem et subordinationem, nam potentiae sensitivae sunt veluti participationes quaedam virtutis intellectivae; ac de his specialiter videtur loqui sanctus Thomas. Adhuc tamen in his propria efficientia non cernitur, sed quaedam veluti causalitas exemplaris, cum cognitio sensitiva sit quaedam imitatio intellectivae, quo etiam modo opera vegetativae partis in quantum fiunt, quasi arte et intellectu, dici possunt illius imitationes.

units.en: A second note. — Lastly it must be observed that between the cognitive and the appetitive powers there seems to be found a certain special order. For as the root of love is cognition, so the root and cause of the appetitive power seems to be the cognitive power. Whence this is a proper demonstration: because a living thing is cognitive, it is appetitive — where the word because can import no other causality than that of effective emanation. It must be said nevertheless that neither between the cognitive and the appetitive power does there intervene properly an effective causality, physical or metaphysical, according to which, one being posited, the other follows because it is necessary to its disposition — not as though it were its proper cause: just as from rationality follows wonder, and from wonder laughter, not because these powers effect one another, but because, one being posited, the other follows, since the act of the one serves in some way the act of the other: and this causality suffices for an a priori demonstration — as immortality is demonstrated a priori through immutability, not because the one is the effective cause of the other, but because they follow upon one another. Add that cognition does not cause love effectively but objectively, by proposing the good; whence neither is it necessary that the appetitive power itself be made effectively by the cognitive, but it is enough that it necessarily presupposes and follows it. Of which matter more at large below in book 5.
units.orig: Notatio altera. — Ultimo est advertendum inter potentias cognoscitivas et appetitivas videri inveniri quemdam specialem ordinem. Nam sicut radix amoris est cognitio, ita radix, et causa appetitivae potentiae, videtur esse potentia cognoscitiva. Unde haec est propria demonstratio: quia vivens est cognoscitivum, est appetitivum: ubi dictio quia, non potest aliam causalitatem importare, quam dimanationis effectivae. Dicendum tamen neque inter potentiam cognoscitivam et appetitivam intercedere proprie causalitatem effectivam physicam, seu metaphysicam, juxta quam uno posito, sequitur aliud, eo quod sit necessarium ad dispositionem illius, non quasi sit propria ejus causa: sicut ex rationalitate sequitur admiratio, et ex admiratione risus, non quia hae potentiae sese efficiant, sed quia una posita sequitur alia, quia actus unius deservit aliquo modo ad actum alterius: atque haec causalitas sufficit ad demonstrationem a priori: sicut immortalitas demonstratur a priori per immutabilitatem, non quia una sit causa effectiva alterius, sed quia se consequuntur. Adde quod cognitio non causat effective amorem, sed objective proponendo bonum, unde etiam non oportet, ut ipsa potentia appetitiva effective fiat a cognoscitiva, sed satis est, quod illam necessario supponat, et sequatur. De qua re latius infra in lib. 5.

sections.titel: Lib. III, cap. XXX — An sit unus tantum sensus interior, an plures

units.en: By what reasoning the common interior sense is proved. — The exterior senses having been explained, it remains to speak of the interior ones, of which matter Aristotle treated in book 3 of De anima, chapters 2 and 3, and the interpreters there; St. Thomas both elsewhere and in the first part, question 78, article 4, where he explains the chief points, but they will be discussed here at somewhat greater length. In this doubt, then, I presuppose that there is an interior sense; on which matter it must be noted that these seven words — sensus communis, phantasia, imaginatio, aestimativa, cogitativa, memoria, reminiscentia — signify a sensitive power distinct from the five explained above, whether manifold or one and the same as it is the principle of diverse acts, of which presently: the common sense, then, is the interior power that knows the proper objects of the exterior senses and discerns between them; and from this discernment above all the common sense was detected by the philosophers, for that operation is most necessary to sensitive nature, and could not belong to any one exterior sense itself, since to discern between two things one must know both: sight indeed discerns between two colors, and hearing between two sounds, but between a sound and a color neither discerns, because neither knows both: the common sense therefore was necessary. Nor can it be said that the same soul discerns through the diverse senses: for it knows only through a power: it must therefore know through the same power, in order to discern them. Aristotle brings another reason in On Sleep and Waking, chapter one: namely that it may know the operations of the external senses — a reason to be accepted in a sound sense, according to what was said in chapter 14.
units.orig: Sensus interior communis qua ratione probetur. — Explicatis sensibus exterioribus, dicendum superest de interioribus, qua de re egit Aristoteles 3, de Anima, cap. 2 et 3, et interpretes ibi, divus Thomas tum alibi, tum 1 p., q. 78, art. 4, ubi praecipua quaeque explicat, sed paulo latius hic erunt disserenda. In hac vero dubitatione suppono, dari sensum interiorem, pro qua re notandum septem haec vocabula, sensus communis, phantasia, imaginatio, aestimativa, cogitativa, memoria, reminiscentia, significare potentiam sensitivam a quinque supra explicatis distinctam, sive multiplicem, sive eamdem, prout est principium diversorum actuum, de quo statim agendum: sensus ergo communis est potentia interior cognoscens objecta propria sensuum exteriorum, discernensque inter illa, ex qua discretione potissime sensus communis a philosophis deprehensus est, illa siquidem operatio maxime necessaria est naturae sensitivae, nec poterat convenire eidem exteriori sensui, cum ad discernendum inter duo oporteat utrumque cognoscere: visus autem discernit quidem inter duos colores, et auditus inter sonos duos, at inter sonum et colorem neuter discernit, quia neuter utrumque cognoscit: necessarius ergo fuit sensus communis. Nec dici potest eamdem animam per diversos sensus discernere: illa enim non nisi per potentiam cognoscit: per eamdem ergo potentiam oportet cognoscat, ut illa discernat. Aliam rationem affert Aristoteles, de Somno et vigilia, capite primo, ut scilicet cognoscat operationes sensuum externorum, quae ratio sano modo est acceptanda, juxta dicta, cap. 14.

units.en: Albert's reason, and formerly St. Thomas's, is excluded. — Albert (Summa de homine, treatise 2, on the common sense, question 2) and St. Thomas (opusculum 43, chapter 4) brought in yet another reason for proving the common sense: namely that it may perceive the common sensibles through species of their own; but this reason certainly supposes something false, because the interior sense does not know the common sensibles otherwise than the exterior does, as we warned in chapter 8, and as St. Thomas also notes in the first part, question 78, article 3, reply to the second, and Avicenna, book 6 of the Naturalia, part 3, chapter 8, at the end, and part 4, chapter 1. Only that first reason, therefore, concludes that there is a common sense; nor is it called common by community of predication, since it is a certain particular power in the animal, but by community of object, insofar as it perceives all the external sensibles, and flows into all the exterior senses as their common principle. So St. Thomas, first part, question 78, article 4, reply to the first; Albert, book 2, treatise 4, chapter 12.
units.orig: Alberti ratio atque olim divi Thomae excluditur. — Aliam quoque rationem probandi sensum communem invexerunt Albertus, Summa de homine, tractatu 2, de Sensu communi, quaest. 2, sanctus Thomas, opusc. 43, cap. 4, nimirum ut percipiat sensibilia communia per proprias species, quae certe ratio falsum supponit: quia sensus interior non aliter cognoscit sensibilia communia, quam exterior, ut cap. 8 monuimus, ac etiam notant divus Thomas, 1 part., quaest. 78, artic. 3, ad 2, Avicenna 6, Naturalium, part. tertia, cap. 8, in fin., et part. 4, cap. 1. Sola ergo prima illa ratio concludit dari sensum communem; neque vero communis dicitur communitate praedicationis, cum sit potentia quaedam particularis in animante, sed communitate objecti, quatenus sensibilia cuncta externa percipit, in omnesque sensus exteriores influit tanquam commune eorum principium. Ita sanctus Thomas, 1 part., quaestion. 78, artic. 4, ad 1. Albertus, libr. secundo, tractat. quarto, capit. decimo secundo.

units.en: A doubt about the common sense, and how Philoponus dispatches it. — It is refuted. — Themistius's dispatch is refuted. — The true solution. — Someone will doubt how one and corporeal power can attain sensibles so diverse and often contrary. Some say that the common sense is indeed indivisible, but that, since it is in an extended organ, it receives the species of the diverse sensibles according to that organ's diverse parts. So Philoponus, on De anima, folio 79. This answer, first, supposes that the species are received in the organ and not in the power, which was disproved above. Secondly it asserts that the said power is indivisible, which is repugnant to a material accident existing in an extended subject. Thirdly it feigns that diverse species are always received in diverse parts. Themistius therefore answers otherwise, book 2 on De anima, chapter 8: the common sense does not receive in itself the species of the sensibles, but judges of the things set before it in the external senses; which Galen too seems to hold, book 7 On the Doctrines, at the end, and Giles, book 2 on De anima, likewise at the end; but the opinion is false, for the common sense judges by knowing, and it cannot perform that unless it receives the species in itself, according to what was treated above. It must be answered, then, that the common sense knows things so various because it is a more perfect and hence more universal power, uniting in itself the virtue of the external senses — as can be established from what was said above, book 2, chapter 2; whence St. Augustine, book 12 on Genesis to the Letter, chapter 26, compares the five senses to as many rivulets flowing from the one common sense as from a fountain. The point about the contrariety of species was already resolved above, in chapter 2.
units.orig: Dubium circa sensum communem quo pacto a Philopono expediatur. — Impugnatur. — Impugnatur expeditio Themistii. — Vera solutio. — Dubitabit aliquis, quomodo potentia una, ac corporea queat attingere sensibilia adeo diversa, et saepe contraria. Quidam aiunt sensum communem esse quidem indivisibilem, attamen cum sit in organo extenso, secundum diversas illius partes recipere species diversorum sensibilium. Ita Philoponus, de Anima, fol. 79. Quae responsio primo supponit species recipi in organo, et non in potentia, quod supra improbatum est. Secundo asserit dictam potentiam esse indivisibilem, quod repugnat accidenti materiali, ac in subjecto extenso existenti. Tertio fingit diversas species recipi semper in diversis partibus: aliter ergo respondet Themistius, lib. 2, de Anima, cap. 8, sensum communem in se non recipere species sensibilium, sed judicare de iis, quae coram se ponuntur in sensibus externis, quod etiam videtur sentire Galenus 7, de Placitis, in fine, Aegidius 2, de Anima, etiam in fine; sed est falsa sententia, nam sensus communis judicat cognoscendo, non potest autem id praestare, nisi species in se recipiat, juxta superius tractata. Respondendum ergo sensum communem tam varia cognoscere, quia est potentia perfectior, atque adeo universalior, uniens in se virtutem sensuum externorum, quod ex supradictis, libr. secundo, capit. secundo, constare potest; unde D. Augustinus 12, super Genesim ad lit., c. 26, quinque sensus totidem comparat rivulis ab uno communi sensu tanquam a fonte manantibus. Illud autem de contrarietate specierum solutum jam superius est in capit. 2.

units.en: The description of the phantasy, and its etymology in the author's judgment. — The phantasy is the interior sense able to know exterior sensibles in their absence: for this operation is common to us with the brutes, and therefore to be attributed to some sense — to that one, surely, which can conserve the species of things sensed, in their absence, and know abstractively through them; and which for that reason is named phantasia, the etymology being taken from light, as Aristotle notes according to the translation of Argyropoulos and Perion, the exposition of St. Thomas, the Commentator, Simplicius, and Themistius in his paraphrase: for light is called in Greek phōs; and because light makes colors appear, thence is derived phasis, that is, first appearing, and then phantasia, because, namely, it makes absent things appear. Philoponus adds that phantasia is so called as being, as it were, the standing of the things that appear, whence he says it is derived from phaos and stasis, which in Greek signifies permanence: for the phantasy retains the species permanently, even in the absence of the object; and so he interprets the text.
units.orig: Phantasiae descriptio, et etymologia ex sententia auctoris. — Phantasia est sensus interior potens cognoscere sensibilia exteriora in eorum absentia: haec quippe operatio nobis est cum brutis communis, ideoque alicui sensui tribuenda: illi certe, qui species rerum sensatarum in absentia valet conservare, ac per illas abstractive cognoscere, quique propterea phantasia nuncupatur, etymologia sumpta a lumine, ut Aristoteles notat juxta translationem Argyropili et Perionii, expositionem divi Thomae, Commentatoris, Simplicii et Themistii in paraphrasi: lumen enim dicitur graece φῶς: quia vero lumen facit apparere colores, inde derivatur φάσις, id est, prima apparitio, ac deinde phantasia, quia scilicet res absentes facit apparere.
