Addit Philoponus phantasiam dici quasi statum eorum, quae apparent, unde ait derivari a φάος, et στάσις, quod graece significat permanentiam: retinet enim phantasia species permanenter, etiam absente objecto, atque ita textum interpretatur.

units.en: A threefold difference of the phantasy from the external senses, from Aristotle. — Being about to define the phantasy, Aristotle first distinguishes it from the other powers, and first from the senses — the external ones, namely — as can be established in the text; and he applies three differences. The first is that although sense is given neither in act nor in potency, the phantasy nevertheless is: as in dreams. You will press: in dreams sense is given in potency. Themistius meets this first, in the paraphrase of the third book of De anima: it is verified conditionally — even were the senses not to remain even in potency, as in a blind man, the phantasy could be saved. Secondly it must be answered that it is verified when in dreams we feign something impossible, of which there is sense neither in act nor in potency. But Aristotle adds that sense is always present, not the phantasy — words which Themistius omits in his paraphrase as difficult; yet they stand in the Greek letter, which St. Thomas expounds so that the intended difference between the powers themselves may not vanish: for he says that sense, that is, the faculty of sensing, is always present, but not the phantasy, that is, its act. Now Simplicius and Philoponus expound that in children there is an exterior sense apt for operating, but not a phantasy: but they contradict experience, for infants dream and imagine, though imperfectly, just as they also operate imperfectly through the exterior senses. Wherefore Avicenna's exposition pleases: that sense is always present to its object, because it knows it only when present; but not so the phantasy, since it knows the object even when absent: whence those words do not add a new difference, but expound the one already laid down. The second difference, then, is that sense is in all animals, but the imagination not likewise — how this is to be understood will be said below. The third difference, that sense is always true about its proper sensible, while the imagination is often false; of which matter above in chapter 10. But you will oppose text 161, in which Aristotle says the imagination is true or false because sense is such: he holds, then, that the falsity of the imagination has its origin from the falsity of sense, and hence that this third difference is null. Philoponus answers well that the phantasy, already in the cognition of simple sensibles, follows — as true and as false, at least occasionally — the sense from which it received them; but because it composes sensibles and feigns impossible things, therein it differs from sense.
units.orig: Differentia triplex phantasiae a sensibus externis ex Aristotele. — Definiturus autem Aristoteles phantasiam, prius eam distinguit ab aliis potentiis, et primo a sensibus nimirum externis, ut in textu constare potest: adhibet autem tres differentias. Prima est, quia licet sensus, neque actu, neque potentia detur, est tamen phantasia: ut in somniis. Instabis in somniis sensum dari in potentia. Occurrit primo Themistius, in paraphrasi libri tertii de Anima, id verificari conditionaliter: esto non manerent sensus etiam potentia, ut in caeco, salvari posse phantasiam. Secundo occurrendum verificari quando in somnis impossibile aliquid fingimus, cujus neque sensus actu est, neque potentia: addit vero Aristoteles sensum semper adesse, non phantasiam, quae verba Themistius in paraphrasi omittit, tanquam difficilia; habentur tamen in graeca littera, quae D. Thomas exponit, ut intenta inter ipsas potentias differentia nulla evadat: ait enim sensum, id est, facultatem sentiendi semper adesse, non tamen phantasiam, id est, actum ejus. Jam vero Simplicius et Philoponus exponunt in pueris esse sensum exteriorem aptum ad operandum, non vero phantasiam: sed repugnant experientiae, nam infantuli somniant et imaginantur, licet imperfecte, sicut et per sensus exteriores imperfecte operantur. Quare Avicennae expositio placet, sensum semper adesse objecto suo, quia non nisi illud praesens cognoscit: phantasiam autem non ita, cum etiam cognoscat objectum absens: unde verba illa non addunt novam differentiam, sed jam positam exponunt. Secunda ergo differentia est: quod sensus cunctis insit animalibus, imaginatio vero non item, de qua quomodo sit intelligenda inferius dicetur. Tertia differentia, quod sensus semper sit verus circa proprium sensibile, imaginatio autem saepe sit falsa, qua de re supra in c. 10. Oppones vero textum 161, in quo Aristoteles ait imaginationem esse veram, aut falsam, quia sensus talis est: sentit ergo imaginationis falsitatem habere originem ex falsitate sensus, atque adeo nullam esse hanc tertiam differentiam. Respondet bene Philoponus, phantasiam jam in cognitione simplicium sensibilium tam veram, quam falsam saltem occasionaliter, sensum sequi, a quo illam acceperat; quia tamen sensibilia componit et impossibilia fingit, in eo differre a sensu.

units.en: The difference of the imagination from opinion. — The difference of the phantasy from opinion, belief, etc. — In the second place he assigns the difference between imagination and opinion: that opinion moves the appetite, but not the imagination. Someone will say: the imagination often causes fear, even when there is no opinion or appearance of an evil to come, as experience seems to teach. On account of this objection some expound the difference thus: from opinion the motion of the appetite always follows; from imagination not always indeed, but sometimes, as when it is strong and vehement — which Aristotle indicates in the example of the picture; for seeing of itself does not move the appetite, but it moves it if the thing be beautiful or horrible. It must be said, however, that the phantasy alone never moves the appetite unless there be mingled with it an opinion of evil or of good, at least as possible: for a vehement apprehension brings it about that we consider the evil as possible for us, whence now, lest it happen, we are in dread. The Philosopher assigns other, easier differences in the same place. Lastly he sets the difference between phantasy, opinion, belief, persuasion and reason; for these four latter are either the same or accompany one another, since where opinion is, there is — or always can be — belief, and persuasion, and reason: but the phantasy is found without them.
units.orig: Differentia imaginationis ab opinione. — Differentia phantasiae ab opinione, fide, etc. — Secundo loco assignat differentiam inter imaginationem et opinionem, quod opinio moveat appetitum, non vero imaginatio. Dicet aliquis: Imaginatio saepe causat timorem, etiamsi nulla sit opinio, vel apparentia mali eventuri, ut experientia docere videtur. Ob hanc objectionem nonnulli exponunt differentiam, ut ex opinione semper sequatur motio appetitus, ex imaginatione non quidem semper, sed aliquando, veluti cum fortis est et vehemens, quod indicat Aristoteles in exemplo de pictura; visio enim per se non movet appetitum, movet autem, si sit pulchra, vel horribilis: dicendum tamen phantasiam solam nunquam movere appetitum, nisi illi misceatur opinio mali, vel boni, saltem ut possibilis: vehemens quippe apprehensio efficit, ut malum tanquam nobis possibile consideremus, unde jam, ne eveniat, formidamus. Alias differentias assignat Philosophus ibidem faciliores. Ultimo ponit differentiam inter phantasiam, opinionem, fidem, suasionem et rationem, nam quatuor haec posteriora, vel idem sunt, vel se comitantur, quia ubi opinio est, ibi est, vel semper esse potest fides, et suasio et ratio: phantasia autem sine iisdem invenitur.

units.en: The description of the phantasy from Aristotle. — The imaginativa. — The aestimativa. — The cogitativa. — Memory. — Reminiscence. — From all these the Philosopher concludes the definition of the phantasy: it is a motion made by sense in act; where it is rather the phantasying that is defined than the phantasy — nay, the definition fits also the act of the common sense, unless you comprehend this act under 'sense in act', as Philoponus expounds: yet perhaps that labor is not needed, because they are not distinct powers, as we shall say below. It is defined more clearly, then, as we said in number 4: the phantasy is the power which receives and conserves the species of the external sensibles, and through them operates in the absence of the object. Other definitions are delivered by the Commentator, in that book, text 160; Albert, book 3 of De anima, treatise 4, chapter 8; Cicero, book 1 of the Academic Questions. Now the imagination nearly coincides with the phantasy, and only adds the power of compounding possibles and of feigning impossibles. The aestimativa is described as the interior sense able to apprehend under the aspect of the agreeable and the disagreeable, or, as they commonly speak, under an unsensed aspect: for this operation too is common to all animals, and can be assigned to no external sense; its office is to move the sensitive appetite, which is moved only by the aspect of the agreeable and the disagreeable: it is therefore called aestimativa because in things themselves it estimates something other than what appears outwardly. The cogitativa many think to be a sensitive power proper to man, able to reason about particulars and to compose and divide: but this exceeds the limits of sensitive virtue, as I said above: the cogitativa therefore signifies nothing else than the very same interior sensitive power discerning between the agreeable and the disagreeable, as it exists in a certain special way in man, and has in him some greater perfection, because it is not named from the mere instinct of nature, but also from a nobler cognition and experience, and is often directed even by reason. Memory is called by Aristotle, in the first chapter of On Memory and Reminiscence, the power which knows past things as already known; and in particular memory is described by some as the power apt to know the same as the aestimativa, but in the absence of the objects: for the brute knows a thing under the aspect of the agreeable and the disagreeable though it does not have it present, and sleeping dogs often bark on account of a like cognition and apprehension. Reminiscence is defined as the power which remembers past particular things, not in a simple manner, but with a certain searching and discourse. Whence many believe this virtue belongs not to the sensitive part but to the intellect; and Aristotle intimates it, at the beginning of the book On Memory and Reminiscence, saying that those who are dull of wit are wont to excel in memory: but Aristotle himself, in chapter 2, openly teaches that the virtue is sensitive, which he also proves from a sign: because those who by reminiscence strive to recollect grow weary in the head; and if the searching cease, what could not be found by laboring is sometimes found: but this indication is fallacious, for the concomitance of the works of intellect and sense with one another suffices for it. I judge, then, that reminiscence is made above all by the intellect, at least as to the discourses and compositions that are mingled with it: but because sense always accompanies the intellect, therefore when the latter runs through diverse places and times, the sense too proceeds from one thing to another by a certain successive apprehension; and such reminiscence of it can be described as: an operation of sense from a previous discourse of the intellect; and therefore he said that those who are strong in wit (as being those who discourse easily) are strong in reminiscence.
units.orig: Phantasiae descriptio ex Aristotele. — Imaginativa. — Aestimativa. — Cogitativa. — Memoria. — Reminiscentia. — Ex his omnibus concludit Philosophus definitionem phantasiae: Est motus factus a sensu in actu; ubi potius phantasiatio definitur, quam phantasia, imo definitio competit etiam actui sensus communis, nisi hunc actum sub sensu in actu comprehendas, ut Philoponus exponit: fortasse tamen id opus non est, eo quod distinctae potentiae non sunt, ut infra dicemus: definitur ergo clarius, ut n. 4 dicebamus, phantasia: potentia, quae species sensibilium externorum recipit et conservat, ac per illas operatur in absentia objecti. Alias definitiones tradit Commentator, illo in libro, textu 160, Albertus 3, de Anima, tractatu 4, cap. 8, Cicero 1, Academicarum quaestionum. Jam vero imaginatio coincidit fere cum phantasia, solumque addit vim componendi possibilia, ac fingendi impossibilia. Aestimativa describitur sensus interior potens apprehendere sub ratione convenientis et disconvenientis, seu, ut communiter loquuntur, sub ratione insensata: haec siquidem operatio communis etiam est omnibus animantibus, nullique sensui externo deputari valet, cujus munus est movere appetitum sensitivum, qui non nisi a ratione convenientis et disconvenientis movetur: ideo ergo aestimativa dicitur, quia in rebus ipsis aliud aestimat, quam quod exterius appareat. Cogitativam multi putant esse potentiam sensitivam propriam hominis, valentem ratiocinari circa particularia, et componere atque dividere: hoc tamen excedit limites virtutis sensitivae, ut supra dixi: cogitativa ergo nihil aliud significat, quam ipsammet potentiam sensitivam interiorem discernentem inter conveniens et disconveniens, prout speciali quodam modo in homine existit, habetque in ipso majorem aliquam perfectionem, quia non ex solo instinctu naturae dicitur, sed etiam ex nobiliori cognitione et experientia, ac saepe etiam a ratione dirigitur. Memoria ab Aristotele, capite primo, de Memoria et reminiscentia, dicitur potentia, quae cognoscit praeterita, ut jam cognita; speciatim vero a quibusdam memoria describitur potentia apta cognoscere idem quod aestimativa, in absentia tamen objectorum: cognoscit enim brutum rem sub ratione convenientis et disconvenientis, licet illam non habeat praesentem, et canes dormientes saepe latrant propter similem cognitionem et apprehensionem. Reminiscentia definitur potentia, quae rerum particularium praeteritarum memoratur, non simplici modo, sed cum quadam indagatione et discursu. Unde multi credunt hanc virtutem non pertinere ad partem sensitivam, sed ad intellectum, insinuatque Aristoteles, in principio libri de Memoria et reminiscentia, dicens eos, qui sunt hebetes ingenio, solere memoria praestare: verum ipse Aristoteles, cap. 2, aperte docet virtutem esse sensitivam, quod a signo etiam probat: quoniam, qui per reminiscentiam conantur recordari, lassantur capite, quod si indagatio cesset, solet interdum, quod laborando non potuit, inveniri: hoc vero indicium fallax est, ad hoc enim satis est concomitantia operum inter se intellectus atque sensus. Existimo ergo reminiscentiam potissime fieri ab intellectu, saltem quantum ad discursus et compositiones, quae illi commiscentur: quia vero sensus comitatur semper intellectum, ideo quando hic per diversa loca et tempora discurrit, sensus etiam per quamdam successivam apprehensionem ab una in aliam procedit; describique potest talis ejus reminiscentia: operatio sensus a praevio discursu intellectus; ideoque dixit, qui pollent ingenio (utpote qui facile discurrant) pollere reminiscentia.

units.en: The first opinion in the present chapter. — The second opinion. — The third opinion. — The fourth opinion. — The fifth opinion. — The sixth opinion. — These things laid down: about the question of this chapter there are diverse opinions; for some posit only two distinct interior senses, yet declare it in diverse ways: some of them hold the common sense by itself alone to be one power, and the phantasy to be the other, identified with the aestimativa, the cogitativa, the memory, etc.; so Perez, book 3 on De anima, chapter 3, question 14, citing Turisanus, book 2 on the Art of Galen, comment 17, likewise Venetus, on the cited place of De anima. Others say the common sense and the phantasy make the same power, and constitute the aestimativa, cogitativa, memory, etc., as the other: so Marcellus, in the first book of his Traditions. The second principal opinion, third in order, asserts three interior powers: the phantasy, which they say is identified with the common sense; the cogitativa, which they call reason; and the memory. So Galen, in the book On the Difference of Symptoms, chapter 3; Gregory of Nyssa, On the Powers of the Soul, chapters 6 and 7; Damascene, book 2 of the Faith, chapters 17 and 20; Nemesius, On the Nature of Man, chapter 6; Valles, book 2 of the Controversies. But it must be observed that Galen by the word reason signifies the intellect itself, which he falsely believed to be an organic power, as appears from book 7 On the Doctrines, chapter 4, where he writes that the brain has in itself the office of effecting imagination, memory and intellection; but it is not credible that the other, catholic authors follow Galen in this sense — rather by the word reason they perhaps understand the cogitativa itself, which by very many is named particular reason. The fourth opinion distinguishes four interior senses, namely the common sense, the phantasy, the aestimativa or cogitativa, and the memory. This St. Thomas taught, first part, question 78, and in the question On the Soul, article 13, and in opusculum 43, chapter 4; and his School follows it, and Averroes had held it before, book 3 of De anima, text 6, Jandun, book 2 of De anima, question 37, and others commonly. The fifth opinion, besides the four senses now named, adds the imaginativa, which it posits as distinct from the phantasy. It is attributed to Avicenna, fen 1, doctrine 6, chapter 5; and Albert follows it, in the Summa de homine, treatise 4, On the Imagination, and book 2 of De anima, treatise 4, chapter 7. The sixth opinion brings in six interior senses, adding to those just named a reminiscence distinct from memory.
units.orig: Prima opinio in praesenti capite. — Secunda opinio. — Tertia opinio. — Quarta opinio. — Quinta opinio. — Sexta opinio. — His positis, circa quaestionem hujus capitis diversae sunt sententiae; quidam enim duos tantum ponunt sensus interiores distinctos, diverso tamen modo id declarant: nam eorum aliqui volunt sensum communem per se solum esse unam potentiam, phantasiam vero esse alteram, identificatam aestimativae, cogitativae, memoriae, etc.; ita Perezius, lib. 3, de Anima, c. 3, q. 14, citans Turisanum, lib. 2, in artem Galeni, commento 17, item Venetus, ad citatum locum de Anima. Alii dicunt sensum communem et phantasiam facere eamdem potentiam: aestimativam vero, cogitativam, memoriam, etc., alteram constituunt: ita Marcellus, libro 1, suarum traditionum. Secunda opinio principalis, ac tertia in ordine, astruit potentias tres interiores: phantasiam, quam dicunt identificari cum sensu communi: cogitativam, quam rationem vocant: et memoriam. Ita Galenus, lib. de Different. symptomatum, c. 3, Gregorius Nyssenus, de Virib. animae, cap. 6 et 7, Damascenus, lib. 2, Fidei, cap. 17 et 20, Nemesius, de Natura hominis, c. 6, Valles 2, Controversiarum. Sed oportet animadvertere, Galenum rationis vocabulo intellectum ipsum significare, quem falso credidit esse potentiam organicam, ut patet ex 7, de Placitis, c. 4, ubi scribit cerebrum habere in se munus efficiendi imaginationem, memoriam, atque intellectionem; non est vero credibile reliquos auctores catholicos in hoc sensu sequi Galenum, sed forte rationis voce intelligunt ipsam cogitativam, quae a plerisque ratio particularis nuncupatur. Quarta opinio distinguit sensus quatuor interiores, nimirum sensum communem, phantasiam, aestimativam, seu cogitativam, et memoriam. Hanc docuit S. Thomas, 1 part., quaest. 78, et quaest. de Anima, art. 13, et opusculo 43, cap. 4, sequiturque illius Schola, et tenuerat antea Averroes 3, de Anima, text. 6, Jandunus 2, de Anima, quaest. 37, et alii communiter. Quinta opinio, praeter quatuor nunc dictos sensus, addit imaginativam, quam ponit a phantasia distinctam. Tribuitur Avicennae, fen. 1, doctrina 6, cap. 5. Sequiturque Albertus, in Summa de homine, tract. 4, de Imaginatione, et 2, de Anima, tract. 4, cap. 7. Sexta opinio sex inducit sensus interiores, addendo proxime dictis reminiscentiam a memoria distinctam.

units.en: The author's judgment on the first opinion. — On the second. — On the third. — The first foundation of the fourth opinion. — The second foundation. — Among these opinions, the first speaks without foundation; for we shall show that by whatever reasoning the common sense is asserted distinct from the phantasy, by the same the phantasy would have to be distinguished from the rest. The second opinion has a probable foundation, which coincides with the foundation of the fourth, as we shall see a little later. The third, next, does not please, because it rests only on experience drawn from medicine, and does not proceed from the thing's own principles — distinguishing the powers, namely, by object and by acts: its foundation will be resolved in the following chapter. Now the fourth opinion, which among those cited is held the more probable, has a twofold foundation. First: that interior sensitive cognition is one thing when made through sensed species, another through unsensed ones, and that the powers knowing through them are diverse: since powers knowing through species of diverse characters must be diverse. And it is confirmed: practical and speculative judgment pertain to diverse powers; but the power knowing through sensed species knows speculatively, without order to pursuit or flight, while that knowing through unsensed species judges practically that a thing is to be fled or pursued, since it attains the thing under the aspect of the agreeable or the disagreeable: therefore, etc. The second foundation is that a sensitive power knowing in the presence of the object must be easily changeable and apprehensive, while a power knowing in absence must be retentive of the species: and that these two cannot belong to one material power, since in corporeal things easy apprehension comes from moisture, retention from dryness — two things which cannot predominate together in one organ. And it is confirmed from the common saying: things united in the higher are divided in the lower: wherefore, etc.
units.orig: Auctoris judicium de prima opinione. — De secunda. — De tertia. — Quartae sententiae fundamentum primum. — Fundamentum secundum. — Inter has opiniones, prima sine fundamento loquitur, nam ostendemus, qua ratione distinctus asseritur communis sensus a phantasia, eadem distinguenda esset a reliquis phantasia. Secunda opinio probabile fundamentum habet, quod coincidit cum fundamento quartae, ut paulo post videbimus. Tertia deinde non placet, quia nititur solum experientia desumpta ex medicina, non vero procedit ex propriis rei principiis, objecto scilicet, et actibus distinguendo potentias: fundamentum autem solvetur sequenti capite. Jam quarta opinio, quae inter citatas probabilior habetur, duplex habet fundamentum. Primum: cognitionem sensitivam interiorem aliam fieri per species sensatas, aliam per non sensatas, ac potentias per eas cognoscentes esse diversas: siquidem potentiae cognoscentes per species diversarum rationum, diversas esse oportet. Et confirmatur, nam judicium practicum et speculativum pertinent ad diversas potentias; sed potentia cognoscens per species sensatas cognoscit speculative, sine ordine ad prosecutionem, vel fugam, cognoscens vero per species non sensatas practice judicat esse fugiendum, vel prosequendum, cum rem attingat sub ratione convenientis vel disconvenientis: ergo, et caetera. Secundum fundamentum est, sensitivam potentiam cognoscentem in praesentia objecti debere esse facile mutabilem et apprehensivam: potentiam vero cognoscentem in absentia debere esse retentivam specierum: ista autem duo non posse convenire potentiae materiali, cum facilis apprehensio in corporalibus proveniat ex humiditate, retentio vero ex siccitate, quae duo praedominari simul nequeunt in uno organo. Et confirmatur ex vulgato proloquio: quae in superioribus sunt unita, in inferioribus dividuntur: quare, etc.

units.en: From the foundations adduced the fourth opinion itself is drawn. — On the fifth opinion. — On the sixth. — From these foundations the opinion of St. Thomas is openly gathered: for to know intuitively through the sensed species of all the external senses one interior sense is necessary, namely the common; but to know abstractively another is required, according to the second foundation, and this is the phantasy. Then, to know intuitively through unsensed species another sense is demanded by the same second foundation, which is named the aestimativa, or cogitativa. Finally, from this same foundation, to know abstractively through those same species yet another sense is required, and the memory is posited: therefore, etc. And hence you will gather how much the foundation of the second opinion is worth, which in this fourth was the first. The fifth opinion, besides all this, considered the twofold cognition of sensibles found in us — one simple, which it attributed properly to the phantasy, the other composite, or imaginary, by which we feign, for instance, a golden mountain, a chimera, and the like — and for this compositive operation it added a third power. And by a like reasoning the sixth opinion adds another power on account of the diverse mode of remembering by reminiscence.
units.orig: Ex allatis fundamentis ipsa quarta opinio eruitur. — De quinta opinione. — De sexta. — Ex his fundamentis aperte colligitur sententia D. Thomae, nam ad cognoscendum intuitive per species sensatas omnium externorum sensuum necessarius est unus interior sensus, nimirum communis: ad cognoscendum vero abstractive alter requiritur, juxta secundum fundamentum, et hic est phantasia. Deinde ad cognoscendum intuitive per insensatas species alius sensus postulatur ex eodem secundo fundamento, qui aestimativa nuncupatur, seu cogitativa. Denique ex hoc ipso fundamento ad cognoscendum abstractive per easdem illas species alius sensus requiritur, poniturque memoria: ergo et caetera. Et hinc colliges quantum valeat fundamentum secundae opinionis, quod in hac quarta primum fuit. Quinta opinio, praeter haec omnia, consideravit duplicem cognitionem sensibilium in nobis inventam, aliam simplicem, quam phantasiae proprie attribuit, aliam vero compositam, seu imaginariam, qua fingimus, verbi gratia, montem aureum, chimaeram, et similia, atque ad hanc compositivam operationem addidit tertiam potentiam. Et consimili ratione sexta opinio aliam addit potentiam propter diversum modum memorandi reminiscendo.

units.en: First note toward the decision. — For the decision of the truth it must be observed that the internal senses are not to be multiplied because one can do more than another, but because the one cannot produce the act of the other; for if two internal senses be posited, of which one can do whatever the other can, and more, this latter will surely be posited superfluously: recourse must therefore be had to operations incompossible in the same power, and according to the variety of such operations so many internal senses will have to be multiplied. Nor should you infer that the exterior senses are then posited superfluously, since whatever they can do, the interior can. For first of all the case is not alike: the exterior senses are as it were particular virtues, to which a universal one had to be added, to strengthen the particular ones themselves and to judge of them all: but within, no such necessity occurs. It is answered next that the antecedent is false: for it is the exterior sense that is immediately changed by the object, not the internal; and so although the interior sense knows whatever the exterior does, yet not through an immediate immutation from the object — and therefore the external senses were necessary, because unless they were changed, the interior power could perceive nothing. Let this foundation then stand, commonly received: that the internal senses are to be multiplied only for those actions which cannot be reduced to the same power.
units.orig: Notatio prima pro decisione. — Pro decisione veritatis est advertendum sensus internos non esse multiplicandos ex eo, quod unus possit plura, quam alius, sed quod alter alterius actum edere nequeat; nam si duo sensus interni statuantur, quorum unus valeat quidquid alius, ac plura, operari superflue sane hic posterior statuetur: ad operationes ergo incompossibiles eidem potentiae est recurrendum, ac pro varietate hujusmodi operationum tot multiplicandi erunt sensus interni. Neque inferas, superflue jam poni sensus exteriores, cum quidquid illi possunt, interior possit. Namque imprimis non est id simile: sensus enim exteriores sunt quasi particulares virtutes, quibus addi debuit universalis, quae particulares ipsas roboraret, ac de omnibus judicaret: interius autem non occurrit talis necessitas. Respondetur deinde antecedens falsum esse: immutatur enim sensus exterior ab objecto immediate, non internus, atque adeo quamvis sensus interior cognoscat quidquid exterior, non tamen per immutationem immediatam ab objecto, ideoque fuerunt necessarii externi sensus, quia nisi immutarentur illi, non posset interior potentia quidquam percipere. Sit ergo constitutum fundamentum, receptum communiter, per eas tantum actiones esse multiplicandos sensus internos, quae ad eamdem potentiam non possunt reduci.

units.en: Second note. — Secondly it must be noted that no more internal senses are to be brought in for man than for the perfect brutes, since in these is found the sensitive nature, which is strong in perfection within that grade: and if some operation is seen more perfect in man, a power is not straightway to be multiplied in him, since that greater perfection can be given within the same species of power. From this foundation St. Thomas excludes the fifth opinion, Avicenna's; for that compositive operation is experienced only in us, and can be attributed to the intellect — or at any rate, for eliciting it, it will be enough that the phantasy of man be posited nobler: from which foundation also the distinction of memory from reminiscence is excluded.
units.orig: Notatio secunda. — Secundo est notandum, non esse in homine inducendos plures sensus internos, quam in brutis perfectis, siquidem in his reperitur natura sensitiva, quae pollet perfectione intra eum gradum: quod si aliqua operatio in homine visitur perfectior, non continuo est in illo multiplicanda potentia, cum ea perfectio major dari valeat intra eamdem potentiae speciem. Ex quo fundamento excludit D. Thomas quintam opinionem Avicennae, nam operatio illa compositiva solum in nobis experitur, attribuique poterit intellectui, vel certe ad illam eliciendam satis erit, quod phantasia hominis ponatur nobilior: ex quo etiam fundamento distinctio memoriae a reminiscentia excluditur.

units.en: First assertion. — It is concluded against the distinction of the common sense from the phantasy, and against the distinction of the aestimativa and the memory. — These things presupposed, let the first conclusion be: it seems more probable that the common sense and the phantasy are not really distinct powers; and the same must be said of the aestimativa and the memory, and universally of the power knowing intuitively and abstractively. The conclusion is proved. A power knowing abstractively must receive the species of the object: either therefore it receives it in the presence of the object, or in its absence: this second is impossible, because external sensibles change the senses only when they exist present to them — whence neither species nor acts last except in their presence: therefore since the phantasy and the memory cannot be changed otherwise than by means of the immutation of the external sense, they must be changed in the presence of the object: they can therefore be changed, and operate, in the presence of the object. This last consequence is clear: for a power that can be changed by a present object can be attentively changed, and hence come forth into act, and that necessarily, since it is a naturally acting power not impeded; wherefore the power that knows in the absence of the object can know in its presence: the powers therefore need not be multiplied on account of these acts: and herewith the foundation of the contrary opinion is destroyed. And the conclusion is confirmed, since these powers would have to be distinguished on the ground that the one apprehends easily and the other retains: but this reason has been destroyed, because as soon as the external sense is changed the phantasy is changed, and hence as easily as can be: these therefore need not be distinguished. Which is further shown, first: for if the phantasy is not changed together with the sense, then after some time has passed it will be changed; but in the meantime what, pray, has happened in the phantasy, whereby it has come out more disposed for the immutation than before? nothing certainly can be assigned, nor likewise can an agent be indicated by which the disposition was produced or the impediment removed. Secondly it is also contrary to experience: otherwise, for the species of a thing to remain in the memory, the thing itself would have to be present to the sense for some time — which is false, because though we see a thing suddenly, if we attend enough, we easily remember it afterwards. Thirdly, because the office of the common sense is to attend and concur with the external senses in their sensations: but this same is the office of the imaginativa, as experience shows, for if we imagine about the same thing which we have present, we by no means sense it — as St. Thomas too and Themistius confess. From these things therefore it is concluded that the common sense and the imagination are not distinguished; for they would be distinguished above all in order to know in presence and in absence: but for this they need not be distinguished, as has been shown: therefore, etc. And this reasoning proves also that the aestimativa and the memory are not distinguished; while to feign diverse internal senses, so that one should know in presence only, and another both in presence and in absence, is superfluous, and against the foundation laid down above.
units.orig: Prima assertio. — Concluditur contra distinctionem sensus communis a phantasia, et contra aestimativae ac memoriae distinctionem. — His suppositis sit prima conclusio. Probabilius videtur sensum communem et phantasiam non esse potentias realiter distinctas, idemque dicendum de aestimativa et memoria, et in universum de potentia intuitive et abstractive cognoscente. Probatur conclusio. Nam potentia cognoscens abstractive objecti speciem debet recipere: vel ergo recipit in praesentia objecti, vel in absentia: hoc secundum est impossibile, quia externa sensibilia tantum immutant sensus, cum illis praesentia existunt. Unde neque species, aut actus durant, nisi in eorumdem praesentia: ergo cum phantasia et memoria aliter non possint immutari, quam media immutatione sensus externi, immutari necesse est in praesentia objecti: possunt ergo immutari, ac operari in praesentia objecti. Ultima haec consequentia liquet: nam potentia quae immutari valet ab objecto praesente, potest attente immutari, ac proinde in actum prodire, idque necessario, cum sit potentia naturaliter agens non impedita; quare potentia in absentia objecti cognoscens potest cognoscere in praesentia: non ergo propter hos actus multiplicari debent potentiae: atque hinc destruitur fundamentum contrariae sententiae. Et confirmatur conclusio, quoniam hae potentiae ideo distinguendae essent, quod una facile apprehendat, altera retineat: haec autem ratio destructa est, quia simulac immutatur sensus externus, immutatur phantasia, atque adeo quam potest facile: non ergo oportet ista distinguere. Quod amplius ostenditur, primo, nam si phantasia non simul cum sensu immutatur, sane transacto aliquo tempore immutabitur; interim vero quid, quaeso, factum est in phantasia, ex quo magis disposita evaserit ad immutationem, quam antea? nihil certe potest assignari, neque item agens indicari, a quo producta sit dispositio, vel ablatum impedimentum. Secundo experientiae quoque adversatur, alioquin ut species rei in memoria maneret, oporteret ut per tempus aliquod res ipsa praesens sensui adesset, quod falsum est, quia licet subito rem videamus, si satis attendimus, facile postea memoramur. Tertio, quia officium sensus communis est attendere et concurrere cum externis sensibus ad eorum sensationes: sed hoc idem est munus imaginativae, ut patet experientia, nam si imaginemur circa eamdem rem, quam praesentem habemus, minime illam sentimus, ut etiam D. Thomas et Themistius fatentur. Ex his ergo concluditur, sensum communem et imaginationem non distingui; maxime enim distinguerentur, ut in praesentia et absentia cognoscerent: ad hoc autem non oportet distingui, ut ostensum est: ergo, etc. Quae ratio probat etiam aestimativam et memoriam non distingui; fingere autem diversos sensus internos, ut unus cognoscat in praesentia tantum, alius vero tum in praesentia, tum in absentia, superfluum est, et contra supra positum fundamentum.

units.en: The second foundation of the fourth opinion, in number 9, is satisfied. — To the second foundation of the fourth opinion some answer that in material things the same thing can be receiver and conserver, as lead the seal's impression. It is answered, however, that in the present case this immutation is not altogether material but intentional, and hence comes about without resistance. Add that the species themselves are received not only in the organ but also in the power itself, from whose nature it comes that they are better or worse conserved in it, though the disposition of the organ contributes somewhat: and experience teaches that in the part of the brain in which the interior sense is placed there is not that diversity of dispositions which the aforesaid opinion demands. To the confirmation it is answered that that axiom is true when a necessity of dividing the powers is detected — but here none is detected.
units.orig: Satisfit fundamento secundo quartae sententiae, in num. 9. — Ad secundum vero fundamentum quartae sententiae occurritur a quibusdam, in materialibus idem esse posse recipiens et conservans, ut plumbum sigillationem. Respondetur tamen, in praesenti immutationem hanc non esse omnino materialem, sed intentionalem, fierique proinde sine resistentia. Adde species ipsas non tantum recipi in organo, sed etiam in potentia ipsa, ex cujus natura provenit, ut in ea melius, vel deterius conserventur, quamvis nonnihil conducat organi dispositio: atque experientia docet in parte cerebri, in qua collocatur sensus interior, non dari illam diversitatem dispositionum, quae a praedicta sententia exigitur. Ad confirmationem respondetur illud axioma verum esse, quando necessitas deprehenditur dividendi potentias, hic vero deprehendi nullam.

units.en: Second assertion. — It is proved. — To the first foundation of the fourth opinion, in number 9. — Second conclusion: it is more probable that the aestimativa and the memory are not really distinguished from the phantasy. It is proved first: because the distinction of species into sensed and unsensed is vain, as we showed above: therefore that of the powers too. Secondly, granted that distinction of species be admitted, the power knowing a thing under an unsensed aspect must necessarily know it under the sensed aspect as well: therefore such powers are not distinguished. The antecedent is proved: for the power that knows the wolf as an enemy knows it so by no other reasoning or manner than by knowing its exterior accidents, and thus under a sensed aspect: it must therefore necessarily know it so. You will say it is enough if one power know the wolf as such, so that another power judge it to be an enemy: but this evasion is not intelligible, for that judgment — this one is an enemy — intrinsically includes the cognition of the one who bears the enmity: they are not therefore separable acts, pertaining to diverse powers. It is confirmed: the common sense could not judge between diverse sensibles unless it knew both extremes, according to Aristotle and all the philosophers: therefore neither could the aestimativa judge this one to be an enemy unless it knew him. Thirdly I argue: the aspects of the agreeable or the disagreeable are unsensed; but the phantasy knows the thing under some such aspect: therefore one and the same power suffices for both, and so it is not severed from the aestimativa. The last consequence holds from the notes laid down above: the minor is proved, for the phantasy moves the sensitive appetite, to which it is compared as the practical intellect to the will, on the witness of Aristotle, book 3 of De anima, chapter 6, text 44, and chapter 7 throughout; but the appetite is moved by the aspect of the agreeable or the disagreeable: therefore the phantasy itself proposed such an aspect, and knew it. And herewith the first foundation of the fourth opinion in number 9 is resolved: for that distinction of sensed and unsensed species is denied; it is denied likewise that the cognition of such aspects is so diverse as to argue diverse powers; it is denied finally that practical and speculative judgment are made by diverse powers, since they are made much better by the same — the one, namely, having its foundation in the other.
units.orig: Secunda assertio. — Probatur. — Ad primum fundamentum quartae opinionis, in num. 9. — Secunda conclusio. Probabilius est aestimativam et memoriam non distingui realiter a phantasia. Probatur primo: quia distinctio specierum in sensatas et non sensatas vana est, ut supra ostendimus: ergo et potentiarum. Secundo, esto illa specierum distinctio admittatur, potentia cognoscens rem sub ratione insensata, cognoscere illam debet necessario sub ratione etiam sensata: ergo potentiae tales non distinguuntur. Probatur antecedens: nam potentia cognoscens lupum ut inimicum, non alia ratione aut modo ita cognoscit, nisi cognoscendo accidentia exteriora illius, ac adeo sub ratione sensata: debet ergo ita necessario cognoscere. Dices sat esse, si una potentia cognoscat lupum ut sic, ut alia potentia judicet esse inimicum: haec tamen evasio non intelligitur, nam judicium illud, hic est inimicus, includit intrinsece cognitionem ipsius, qui inimicitiam gerit: non sunt ergo actus separabiles, ad diversasque potentias pertinentes. Confirmatur: nam sensus communis non posset judicare inter diversa sensibilia, nisi cognosceret utrumque extremum, secundum Aristotelem et omnes Philosophos: ergo nec aestimativa posset judicare hunc esse inimicum, nisi ipsum cognosceret. Tertio argumentor: rationes convenientis, vel disconvenientis sunt non sensatae, sed phantasia cognoscit rem sub tali aliqua ratione: ergo una eademque potentia ad utrumque sufficit, atque adeo ab aestimativa non secernitur. Ultima consequentia valet ex notationibus supra positis: minor vero probatur, nam phantasia movet appetitum sensitivum, ad quem comparatur, sicut intellectus practicus ad voluntatem, teste Aristotele 3, de Anima, cap. 6, textu 44, et cap. 7, per totum; appetitus autem movetur a ratione convenientis, vel disconvenientis: ergo ipsa phantasia rationem ejusmodi proposuit, ac cognovit. Atque hinc solvitur fundamentum primum quartae opinionis in num. 9: negatur enim distinctio illa specierum sensatarum et non sensatarum: negatur item cognitionem talium rationum tam diversam esse, ut diversas arguat potentias: negatur denique judicium practicum et speculativum fieri a potentiis diversis, cum melius multo fiant ab eadem, uno scilicet in altero fundamentum habente.

units.en: Third assertion. — Third conclusion: it seems more probable that the interior sense is really one only. From what has been said it is concluded thus: the common sense and the phantasy coincide in one power, likewise the aestimativa and the memory between themselves; while the cogitativa, reminiscence and imagination do not add to the number, as was observed above, and only signify diverse perfections of the same sense in man: therefore, etc. And this plainly was Aristotle's opinion, since in the first chapter of On Memory he said the phantasm is an affection of the common sense, and in that whole chapter he speaks of the common sense and the phantasy — nay, of the whole internal power of sensing — as of one, and there pronounces that by the same part we know magnitude, motion and time, and adds that all these things seem to pertain to that primary, princely sense, of which he adds below that it is itself the one that remembers, etc.; he posits, then, only one first, princely interior sense. And in the book On Dreams, chapter 1, he writes that the power of imagining is the same in number as the power of sensing, though diverse in essence and account; where, comparing the imagination with the external senses, he means the power to be the same in number insofar as the imagination and the exterior sense come together after the manner of one virtue for perfect sensing — which office is certainly proper to the common sense, as all hand down. Aristotle therefore attributes the office of the common sense to the imaginativa, and so judges that they are not distinguished. In the same place too he says the external senses change the princely common sense in waking and in dreams in diverse ways — in waking, namely, actually; in dreams through species already received before: he teaches, then, that the common sense conserves the received species, which is the office of the phantasy. And this St. Thomas also intimates, first part, question 84, article 8, reply to the second, saying that in sleep the common sense is sometimes released, and judges; whereas in the Prima Secundae, question 15, article 1, and question 17, article 7, reply to the third, he writes that the common sense is changed only in the presence of the object; and therefore that place of the first part is expounded by his disciples, lest he seem to contradict himself. Again, that the phantasy is not distinguished from the aestimativa according to Aristotle is plain, since the aestimativa is posited as the faculty knowing the aspect of the agreeable and disagreeable and moving the appetite. Whence St. Thomas, first part, question 78, article 4, and more clearly on the second book, distinction 23, question 2, article 4, in the body, and elsewhere, says the aestimativa is compared to the sensitive appetite as the practical intellect to the will: but it has been shown that according to Aristotle the phantasy knows the aspect of the agreeable and moves the appetite, and is compared to it as the practical intellect to the will: therefore according to him the phantasy is not distinguished from the aestimativa. Finally, that the phantasy and the memory are not distinguished is Aristotle's opinion, On Memory, chapter 1, where he openly says the imaginativa is the memory conserving the species — which all admit of the sensed species; but there are no other, unsensed ones, as we have proved: therefore, etc.
units.orig: Tertia assertio. — Tertia conclusio. Probabilius videtur sensum interiorem unum tantum esse realiter. Hoc ex dictis ita concluditur: sensus communis et phantasia in unam coincidunt potentiam, aestimativa item ac memoria inter se; cogitativa autem, reminiscentia et imaginatio non ponunt in numero, ut supra est observatum, solumque significant diversas perfectiones ejusdem sensus in homine: ergo, etc. Et haec plane fuit sententia Aristotelis, cum capite primo de Memoria dixerit phantasma esse affectum sensus communis, atque in toto eo capite de sensu communi, ac phantasia, imo et de virtute tota interna sentiendi tanquam de una loquitur, ibidemque pronuntiat eadem nos parte cognoscere magnitudinem, motum, ac tempus, et subdit, videri haec omnia ad primarium illum principem sensum pertinere, de quo inferius addit, ipsum esse qui memoratur, etc.; unum ergo tantum ponit primum sensum principem interiorem. Et lib. de Insomniis, cap. 1, scribit vim imaginandi eamdem numero esse cum potentia sentiendi, essentia tamen et ratione diversam; ubi imaginationem comparans sensibus externis, vult esse eamdem numero vim, quatenus imaginatio et sensus exterior per modum unius virtutis conveniunt ad perfecte sentiendum: quod certe munus proprium est sensus communis, ut omnes tradunt. Tribuit ergo Aristoteles munus sensus communis imaginativae, atque adeo judicat non distingui: ibidem quoque ait sensus externos immutare principem sensum communem in vigilia et in insomniis diversimode, in vigilia nimirum actualiter, in insomniis autem per species jam ante acceptas: docet ergo sensum communem conservare acceptas species, quod est munus phantasiae. Et hoc insinuat etiam D. Thomas, 1 part., quaest. 84, art. 8, ad secundum, aiens, quod in somno aliquando solvitur communis sensus, ac judicat; cum tamen 1, 2, q. 15, a. 1, et q. 17, a. 7, ad tertium, scribat sensum communem immutari solum in praesentia objecti; et ideo ille locus primae partis ab illius discipulis exponitur, ne sibi adversari videatur. Item quod phantasia ab aestimativa non distinguatur secundum Aristotelem patet, quoniam aestimativa ponitur facultas cognoscens rationem convenientis ac disconvenientis, movensque appetitum. Unde D. Thomas, 1 part., quaest. 78, art. 4, et clarius in 2, dist. 23, quaest. 2, art. 4, in corpore, et alibi, ait aestimativam comparari ad appetitum sensitivum, sicut intellectum practicum ad voluntatem: ostensum est autem, quod secundum Aristotelem phantasia cognoscat rationem convenientis, moveatque appetitum, compareturque ad illum sicut intellectus practicus ad voluntatem: ergo secundum illum phantasia ab aestimativa non distinguitur. Denique, quod phantasia et memoria non distinguantur, est sententia Aristotelis, de Memoria, c. 1, ubi palam ait imaginativam esse memoriam conservantem species; quod omnes admittunt de sensatis; non sunt vero aliae non sensatae, ut probavimus: ergo, etc.

units.en: A double objection against the last assertion is removed. — Nor does anything stand against this conclusion which has not already been resolved, unless perhaps this: that it is proper to material powers to be determined to particular objects, and to be divided into several. Likewise this: that the conclusion delivered is not only not common, but rather contrary to the common one. To the first I answer that in the particular sensitive powers there is indeed found determination and division by particular objects; but in a power universal even within the sensitive grade there is no necessity, nor reason for feigning a division: only in comparing this power to a higher one, that is, the intellect, is it found limited to a more particular object — and that this is consonant with the imperfection of a material power, and with the perfection it can have in its own kind. To the second I answer first that there is no part of our opinion which is not asserted by many; and since they disagree among themselves, room is given us to take from each what seems to us truer, and to consent wholly to none of them. Add secondly that Aristotle stands on our side.
units.orig: Duplex objectio contra proximam assertionem removetur. — Nec aliquid obstat huic conclusioni, quod jam solutum non sit, nisi fortasse illud: proprium esse potentiarum materialium, ut determinentur ad particularia objecta, dividanturque in plures. Item illud: traditam conclusionem non solum communem non esse, sed potius communi adversari. Ad primum respondeo in potentiis quidem sensitivis particularibus inveniri determinationem et divisionem per particularia objecta: in potentia autem intra gradum etiam sensitivum universali, necessitatem non dari, aut rationem fingendi divisionem: solumque comparando hanc potentiam ad altiorem, hoc est, intellectum, deprehendi limitatam ad objectum magis particulare, idque consonum esse imperfectioni potentiae materialis, ac perfectioni, quam in suo genere habere potest. Ad secundum respondeo primo nullam esse partem nostrae sententiae, quae a multis non asseratur; cumque ipsi inter sese dissentiant, locum nobis dari comprehendendi ex quolibet id quod nobis verius videatur, ac nulli eorum in totum consentire. Adde secundo Aristotelem stare a nobis.

units.en: Fourth assertion, denying even a formal distinction among the internal senses. — You will doubt, however, whether at least a formal distinction of the internal senses is to be admitted. It seems it should be affirmed, because diverse definitions can there be delivered: for the common sense is called the power judging of all sensibles in their presence, the phantasy that judging of the same in absence, etc.; and diverse definitions distinguish powers at least formally. Yet let the fourth conclusion be: the interior sense is one adequate power really and formally, and distinct only in inadequate aspects — insofar, namely, as it is compared to diverse acts and is conceived by inadequate concepts. It is proved: that power is formally one in the aforesaid way which has one adequate formal object, about which it exercises a certain genus of acts; for partial objects, and the particular characters of diverse acts, do not argue diverse formal characters of powers: but so stands the matter in the interior sensitive power: therefore, etc. It is explained further and confirmed: in the intellective part there are several names signifying the intellect — as reason, memory, practical intellect, speculative, etc. — and yet there is formally only one power there; and the like holds of the will. Finally, in that manner more than six powers could be formally numbered, as will easily appear to one considering the diversity of the acts of the internal sense. It must be concluded, then, that there is one sense exercising all these acts, which by us is called by diverse names, and circumscribed by inadequate definitions.
units.orig: Quarta assertio, distinctionem etiam formalem negans in sensibus internis. — Dubitabis tamen, an formalis saltem distinctio sensuum internorum sit admittenda? Videtur enim affirmandum, quia possunt ibi diversae definitiones tradi: sensus enim communis dicitur potentia judicans de omnibus sensibilibus in eorum praesentia, phantasia judicans de eisdem in absentia, etc.; definitiones autem diversae distinguunt potentias saltem formaliter. Sit tamen quarta conclusio: Sensus interior una est adaequata potentia realiter et formaliter, solumque in inadaequatis rationibus distincta, quatenus scilicet ad diversos actus comparatur, et conceptibus inadaequatis concipitur. Probatur, quoniam illa potentia est formaliter una praedicto modo, quae unum habet objectum formale adaequatum, circa quod exercet certum genus actuum; partialia namque objecta, particularesque rationes actuum diversorum, diversas rationes formales potentiarum non arguunt: sic autem res habet in potentia sensitiva interiori: ergo, etc. Explicatur amplius et confirmatur: nam in parte intellectiva plura sunt nomina significantia intellectum, ut ratio, memoria, intellectus practicus, speculativus, etc., et tamen ibi una tantum est potentia formaliter; et simile est de voluntate. Denique illo modo potentiae formaliter ultra sex numerari possent, ut facile patebit consideranti diversitatem actuum interni sensus. Concludendum ergo unum esse sensum omnes hos actus exercentem, qui a nobis diversis nominibus nuncupatur, inadaequatisque definitionibus circumscribitur.

sections.titel: Lib. IV, cap. VII — Utrum intellectus noster pro hoc statu pendeat in operatione sua ab operatione phantasiae

units.en: For this whole chapter see the author, book 2, On Grace, chapter 4. — First argument of the denying side. — Second argument. — Third. — Of the substance of the act of our intellect nothing remains to be said beyond what was delivered in the third book; and of the composition and artifice of the acts of the intellect enough has been said in dialectic: it only remains, then, to speak of the mode of operating which our intellect has: and the discourse will be of the intellect in the state of the soul joined to the body; for of the mode of understanding in the other state it is spoken below, in the sixth book. Now in the present question it is certain that the intellect depends on the senses in the acquisition of species, as was shown above. It remains to investigate, however, whether after the acquisition it can freely use them without any dependence on the senses. And indeed, when the external senses are doing nothing, the affirmative answer is plain, as experience teaches, and above all in contemplative men who suffer ecstasy: for Aristotle, Ethics book 7, chapter 1, teaches that divine and heroic men are so given over to contemplation that no other action or affection of the senses remains to be attributed to them. But whether the intellect depends on the internal sense, or phantasy, the negative side seems true here too. First, because the intellect is already constituted in first act through the species, as we hold, and is a power more perfect than the phantasy itself, having of itself virtue and light sufficient for operating: there is no reason, then, why it should depend on the phantasy; whence Aristotle, book 3 of De anima, text 8, and book 2, chapter 5, says that the intellect, once knowledge has been acquired, can operate when it wills, and needs no extrinsic mover. Secondly, the intellect often understands things of which the phantasy has no likenesses — such as common things, spiritual things, etc.: therefore in that operation at least it does not depend on the phantasy. Thirdly, because otherwise the intellect at least would be impeded from its operation when the external senses are bound; for then the phantasy too will be bound — nay, the exterior sense itself could not be bound unless the phantasy were bound, which is as it were the principle of all exterior sensation: but the consequent is against what has been said: therefore, etc.
units.orig: Pro toto hoc capite videndus auctor, l. 2, de Gratia, cap. 4. — Argumentum primum partis negantis. — Argumentum secundum. — Tertium. — De substantia actus intellectus nostri nihil dicendum superest, praeter tradita in libro tertio; de compositione autem et artificio actuum intellectus sufficienter in dialectica dictum est: solum ergo restat dicendum de modo operandi, quem intellectus noster habet: eritque sermo de intellectu in statu animae conjunctae corpori; nam de modo intelligendi in statu altero, infra dicetur libro sexto. Est autem in praesenti quaestione certum intellectum dependere a sensibus in acquisitione specierum, ut supra ostensum est. Investigandum tamen superest, an post acquisitionem possit libere illis uti absque ulla dependentia a sensibus? Et quidem sensibus externis nihil operantibus, plana est responsio affirmans, ut experientia docet, et maxime in viris contemplativis, qui exstasim patiuntur: Aristoteles enim 7 Ethic., cap. 1, docet viros divinos et heroicos ita subditos esse contemplationi, ut nulla alia sensuum actio, seu affectio illis supersit tribuenda: an vero intellectus ab interno sensu, seu phantasia dependeat, videtur pars negativa etiam vera. Primo, quia intellectus constitutus jam est in actu primo per species, ut ponimus, estque potentia perfectior ipsa phantasia, habensque ex se virtutem et lumen sufficiens ad operandum: non est ergo cur a phantasia dependeat; unde Aristoteles 3, de Anima, text. 8, et lib. 2, cap. 5, ait intellectum acquisita jam scientia posse operari cum vult, neque indigere extrinseco motivo. Secundo intellectus saepe intelligit ea, quorum phantasia nullas habet similitudines, veluti rerum communium, spiritualium, etc.: ergo in ea operatione saltem non pendet a phantasia. Tertio, quia alias impediretur saltem intellectus a sua operatione ligatis externis sensibus; tunc enim et phantasia ligabitur, imo exterior ipse sensus ligari non posset, nisi ligata phantasia, quae est quasi principium omnis exterioris sensationis: consequens autem est contra dicta: ergo, etc.

units.en: The various opinions of authors. — In this matter Albert, book 3 of De anima, treatise 2, chapter 19, opines that the intellect, once the species are acquired, has no dependence on the senses, above all in the cognition of spiritual things. Philoponus believes the same, at text 30, and book 3, chapter 4; Thienensis, at text 39; Averroes, Avicenna, Simplicius, Themistius agree, on book 3 of De anima, in the places cited in the preceding chapter; for they say that in common operations the intellect depends on the phantasy, but in the most abstract cognition of God and the angels not at all. Bonaventure too asserted that in the highest contemplation the intellect can be wholly abstracted from the senses, even the interior ones, and contemplate God without any image whatever. Others said that at least in the cognition of itself and of its own species the intellect does not depend on the phantasy. Venetus, at text 33, held that whenever the intellect operates through species elicited from phantasms it does depend on the phantasy, but not when it operates through those which it has formed for itself.
units.orig: Varia auctorum placita. — Hac in re Albertus, lib. 3, de Anima, tractat. 2, cap. 19, opinatur intellectum acquisitis speciebus non habere dependentiam a sensibus, maxime in cognitione spiritualium. Idem credit Philoponus, textu 30, et lib. 3, cap. 4; Thienensis, text. 39; consentiunt, in 3, de Anima, Averroes, Avicenna, Simplicius, Themistius, locis citatis cap. praecedenti; aiunt enim in communibus operationibus pendere intellectum a phantasia, in cognitione vero abstractissima Dei et Angelorum minime. Bonaventura quoque asseruit in altissima contemplatione posse intellectum omnino abstrahi a sensibus etiam interioribus, ac sine ulla prorsus imagine Deum contemplari. Alii dixerunt in cognitione saltem sui, ac suarum specierum non pendere intellectum a phantasia. Venetus, in text. 33, voluit, quoties intellectus per species elicitas a phantasmatibus operatur, pendere quidem a phantasia, non item quando operatur per eas, quas ipse sibi formavit.

units.en: The common conclusion. — The a priori reason from St. Thomas is impugned by Scotus. — The common opinion, however, teaches the opposite — what in Aristotle's phrase is usually said: that the intellect understands nothing except by a turning, not indeed of itself, but of the soul, or of the phantasy, to the phantasms. So St. Thomas, first part, question 84, article 7; Cajetan on the same place; Ferrariensis on book 1 of the Contra Gentes, chapter 65, and book 2, chapter 73; Scotus, on the fourth book, distinction 45, question 2; Giles, book 3 of De anima, text 38. Let the conclusion then be: the soul, while it is united to the body, has an intrinsic dependence on the phantasy, insofar, namely, as it in no wise operates through the intellect unless it also actually operates through some phantasm — which Aristotle expressed in book 3 of De anima, text 39, saying: whoever contemplates must contemplate together with a phantasm. The same is held by St. Dionysius, chapter 7 of the Divine Names, and of the Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 1: It is impossible, he says, for the divine ray to shine upon us unless wrapped about with the variety of the sacred veils. The same St. Augustine, book 4 on Genesis to the Letter, chapter 7, when he says that when we know number, the corporeal sense attains one thing, the reason another; and Nazianzen, oration 2, On Theology. Experience also teaches it: first, because when the phantasy is injured, the use of reason too is injured, and when it is impeded by sleep, the intellect too is impeded: it has therefore a manifest dependence. Secondly: when we strive to understand something perfectly, we form a sensible image of it within ourselves; when we would teach another, we seek sensible examples, as it were supplying matter to the phantasy, on which the intellect depends in learning. These experiences, indeed, adduced by St. Thomas in the cited article 7, show the conclusion certain a posteriori: yet the a priori reason is rendered with difficulty. St. Thomas himself adduces this one: that the object of our intellect is the quiddity of a material thing, which cannot be known by our intellect according to the mode it has in singulars without the help of sense; and that therefore for the perfect cognition of the thing the concomitance of the sensitive operation is demanded. This reason is impugned with many arguments by Scotus, on the fourth book, distinction 3, question 3, nor does it much please me: for it rests chiefly on this, that the intellect does not directly know singulars — which was disproved in chapter 3. Moreover, though it did not know them so, still from the reason adduced no necessary concomitance between the operation of the intellect and that of the phantasy can be had: at its strongest, that reason avails to urge that the intellect needs the help of sense for the perfect cognition of a singular and material thing down to its very singularity: but from this how can so great a dependence be understood or gathered as there is between sense and intellect? How likewise can a reason be had why, the phantasy being injured, the intellect is injured in its operations universally?
units.orig: Communis conclusio. — Ratio a priori ex S. Thoma impugnatur ab Scoto. — Communis tamen sententia oppositum docet, quod Aristotelis phrasi dici solet, intellectum nihil nisi conversione, non quidem sui, sed animae, seu phantasiae ad phantasmata intelligere. Ita S. Thomas, 1 part., quaest. 84, art. 7, Cajetanus ibid., Ferrarius 1, contra Gentes, cap. 65, et lib. 2, cap. 73, Scotus, in 4, distinct. 45, quaest. 2, Aegidius 3, de Anima, text. 38. Sit ergo conclusio: Anima dum corpori unitur, intrinsecam dependentiam habet a phantasia, quatenus videlicet per intellectum minime operatur, nisi actu etiam per phantasma aliquod operetur, quod Aristoteles 3, de Anima, text. 39, expressit, dicens: Qui contemplatur, necesse est una cum phantasmate contempletur. Idem sentit divus Dionysius, c. 7, de Divinis nominibus, et de coelesti Hierarch., cap. 1: Impossibile, inquit, est nobis superlucere divinum radium, nisi varietate sacrorum velaminum circumvolutum. Idem D. Augustinus 4, super Genesim ad litteram, cap. 7, dum ait, quando numerum cognoscimus, aliud corporeum sensum, aliud rationem attingere: et Nazianzenus, orat. 2, de Theologia. Experientia quoque ita docet: primo, quia laesa phantasia, laeditur et rationis usus, eademque impedita somno, impeditur et intellectus: habet ergo manifestam dependentiam. Secundo: quando aliquid perfecte intelligere conamur, sensibilem imaginem illius intra nos formamus; quando alterum docere volumus, sensibilia exempla quaerimus, quasi materiam phantasiae suppeditantes, a qua intellectus in discendo pendet. Quae profecto experientiae a D. Thoma citato, art. 7, allatae ostendunt conclusionem certam a posteriori: attamen ratio a priori difficile redditur. Idem S. Thomas hanc adducit: quod objectum intellectus nostri sit quidditas materialis rei, quae ab intellectu nostro cognosci nequit secundum modum, quem in singularibus habet, absque sensus juvamine, ideoque ad perfectam rei cognitionem postulari concomitantiam sensitivae operationis. Quae ratio multis impugnatur ab Scoto, in 4, dist. 3, q. 3, neque satis mihi arridet: fundatur siquidem potissime in eo, quod intellectus singularia directe non cognoscat, quod, cap. 3, improbatum est. Praeterea quamvis ea non ita cognoscat, attamen adducta ratione non potest haberi necessaria concomitantia inter operationem intellectus et phantasiae: sed cum maxime valet, ea ratio ad suadendum valet, egere intellectum juvamine sensus ad perfectam cognitionem rei singularis ac materialis ad suam usque singularitatem: hinc autem quomodo potest intelligi aut colligi tanta dependentia, quanta est inter sensum et intellectum? Quomodo item haberi ratio, quare laesa phantasia laedatur intellectus in suis operationibus universim?

units.en: Nor do the reasons Scotus adduces please. — See book 6, On the Work of the Six Days, chapter 9, number 7. — A more convenient reason. — Wherefore Scotus brought in other reasons. The first is that this dependence was given in punishment of sin; but the reason falsely supposes that the said dependence is not natural but descends from sin, since it would have place even in the very state of innocence. The second: that such a dependence arises solely from the subordination of the soul's powers, by reason of which they have such a natural connection that, one power operating about some object, the others too operate which are born to attain the same object. But neither does this reason seem to satisfy. First, because it labors in a certain manner under a begging of the principle: for it is the cause of this order and connection that we are seeking. Secondly, because from this, at most, it could be had that the operating intellect excites the phantasy to operate together with it; not, however, that the intellect in its own operation depends on the phantasy, as we experience: nor likewise is a reason rendered why the injury of one redounds upon the other. Wherefore that more convenient and more evident reason presents itself: that the dependence of which we treat comes from the imperfection of the state, in which the intellect does not receive species except while the phantasy actually operates, and both powers are rooted in the same soul, and hence mutually serve one another, and are also a hindrance to one another. Whence when the phantasy is injured and goes mad, it drags with it the intellect and the soul's attention — by which reason alone could the injury redound upon the intellect, incorruptible as it is: the perfection of the imagination too can profit the intellect, because the better the imaginativa apprehends, the better the species that are impressed on the intellect: but the intellect itself also, by operating, moves and draws the imagination with it. Hence, then, arises between these powers so natural a concomitance — which is not essential, but proceeding from actual operation, since in the separated soul, or after the resurrection of bodies, there will be no necessary dependence of the intellect on the phantasy.
units.orig: Neque quae Scotus adducit, placent. — Vide l. 6, de Opere sex dierum, cap. 9, num. 7. — Commodior ratio. — Quare Scotus rationes alias invexit. Prima est, in poenam peccati datam fuisse hanc dependentiam; falso tamen supponit ratio dictam dependentiam naturalem non esse, sed ex peccato descendere, cum in ipso etiam innocentiae statu locum haberet. Secunda, ejusmodi dependentiam solum nasci ex subordinatione potentiarum animae, ratione cujus naturalem connexionem habent talem, ut operante una potentia circa aliquod objectum, operentur et aliae, quae idem objectum natae sunt attingere. Sed nec ratio haec videtur satisfacere. Primo, quia principii petitione quodammodo laborat: nam hujus ordinis et connexionis causam quaerimus. Secundo, quia hinc, ut plurimum, haberi posset intellectum operantem excitare phantasiam, ut cum ipso simul operetur; non tamen haberi, quod in sua ipsius operatione pendeat intellectus a phantasia, ut experimur: neque item ratio redditur cur laesio unius redundet in alterum. Quapropter illa occurrit commodior et evidentior ratio, quod dependentia, de qua tractamus, proveniat ex imperfectione status, in quo intellectus non recipit species, nisi dum actu phantasia operatur, et ambae potentiae in eadem anima radicantur, sibique proinde mutuo deserviunt, atque etiam sunt impedimento. Unde quando phantasia laeditur et insanit, secum trahit intellectum et animae attentionem, qua solum ratione laesio in intellectum, utpote incorruptibilem, redundare potuit: perfectio quoque imaginationis prodesse potest intellectui, quia quanto melius imaginativa apprehendit, eo meliores species imprimuntur intellectui: sed et intellectus ipse operando movet, ac secum trahit imaginationem. Hinc ergo oritur inter potentias has tam naturalis concomitantia, quae essentialis non est, sed ex actuali operatione proveniens, siquidem in anima separata, aut post corporum resurrectionem, necessaria dependentia intellectus a phantasia nulla erit.

units.en: To the first in number 1. — To the second. — To the third. — To the first argument made at the beginning it is answered that the intellect, constituted in first act, needs no extrinsic mover in order to operate, but on account of its conjunction with the body has a natural concomitance with the corporeal power. To the second: when the intellect is engaged about spiritual things, the imagination busies itself about the things from which it always understands — either the things formally represented in the phantasm, or those which can in some way be deduced from it. So St. Thomas above; Philoponus too, on book 3 of De anima, at text 21, notes that for those understanding divine things the imagination concurs, setting types and figures before them — which certainly is the sound of Dionysius's words adduced above. To the third say: if the external and the internal senses together are impeded from their operation, the intellect too will be impeded, as happens in those asleep; if however the external senses are bound not because of an impediment of the imaginative power, but because of its vehement attention to some disparate thing, then the intellect will not at all be impeded — and so it happens in ecstasy.
units.orig: Ad primum in num. 1. — Ad secundum. — Ad tertium. — Ad primum argumentum in principio factum respondetur intellectum in actu primo constitutum non indigere motore extrinseco ad operandum, propter conjunctionem tamen cum corpore habere naturalem concomitantiam cum corporea potentia. Ad secundum: quando intellectus versatur circa spiritualia, imaginatio negotiatur circa ea, ex quibus semper intelligit, aut quae formaliter repraesentantur in phantasmate, aut quae ex illo modo aliquo deduci possunt. Ita S. Thomas supra; Philoponus quoque 3, de Anima, ad text. 21, notat divina intelligentibus concurrere imaginationem, typos et figuras opponentem: quod certe sonant verba Dionysii superius adducta. Ad tertium dic: si sensus externi simul et interni impediantur a sua operatione, fore ut etiam impediatur intellectus, quemadmodum contingit in dormientibus; si tamen sensus externi ligentur non propter imaginatricis impedimentum, sed ob vehementem attentionem illius ad rem disparatam, tunc intellectum minime impeditum iri, sicque in exstasi contingere.

units.en: An instance is dissolved. — You will urge: the intellect of one asleep is more apt to receive impressions of species from separate substances, and even divine revelations, as St. Thomas delivers in book 2 of the Contra Gentes, chapter 81, and sacred Scripture confirms, commonly teaching that revelations were made to the Prophets in dreams; and yet then the phantasy is bound: therefore concomitance does not always intervene between the two powers. It must be answered that in sleep the intellect is indeed more apt to receive species from God — both because of the greater quiet, and lest that impression of species be referred to the things sensed outwardly, or be attributed to one's own discourse; which the same St. Thomas explained in the Secunda Secundae, question 173, article 3, and On Truth, question 12, article 3, reply to the first: but that it is less apt to bear judgment on the things revealed, because while sleeping we do not by the ordinary law have the free use of reason — as the same doctor noted, first part, question 84, article 8, reply to the second.
units.orig: Instantia diluitur. — Urgebis: Intellectus dormientis aptior est ad recipiendas impressiones specierum a substantiis separatis, ac revelationes etiam divinas, ut S. Thomas tradit 2, contra Gentes, cap. 81, et sacra Scriptura confirmat, communiter docens revelationes in somniis factas fuisse Prophetis; et tamen tunc ligata est phantasia: non ergo inter utramque potentiam semper intercedit concomitantia. Occurrendum, esse quidem in somno intellectum aptiorem ad recipiendas species a Deo: tum propter quietem majorem: tum ne illa impressio specierum referatur ad ea, quae exterius sentiuntur, vel proprio discursui tribuatur, quod idem D. Thomas 2, 2ae, quaest. 173, art. 3, et de Verit., quaest. 12, art. 3, ad 1, explicuit: esse tamen minus aptum ad ferendum judicium de rebus revelatis, quia inter dormiendum liberum usum rationis de lege ordinaria non habemus, sicut idem doctor, 1 part., quaest. 84, art. 8, ad 2, notavit.
